JAI& JoLLY BEGGAR.'. (Archbishop Whateleysaid that " He could thank God he had never given sixpence to a beggar in the street" Of course this was his way of denouncinz indiscriminate charity, and the Archbishop was right.. In the vas- majority of cases the public beggar is a public impostor. Persons who encourage him are lelping to maintain and extend the vast army of professional pauperism. Christ tan men ought to have their rules of action in reference to this matter. 1. They should give a definite proportion of their benevolences to the relief of poverty. 2. They should give their benevolences either after personal in- Vestigation or through tried and trusted agents or agencies. 3. They should never give a penny to any beggar whose case they have not examined. How dis- gusted people would be if they could follow to their haunts some of the whining vagabonds who have abused their kindness. Some times the beggar leaves a well- understood mark on the wall of the house where he has been successful, that others may know whether it is worth their while' to call or not Sometimes, with the accuracy et a .bank clerk, the beggar keeps a classified list of persons in the town, marking them as" good" or "bad," from his (the beggar's) point of view! Generally the lodging-houses in which the professional beggar passes his nights are the scenes of coarse revelry, which would greatly astound those who have been relieving the servile and slippery applicant for "charity." In truth the lines in which Pun described them a while since are only too realistic.] Now, whence come the beggars that knock at our doors?

From their reeking resorts. Their grim alleys and courts, From tenements And dirty " Rents," From lanes Where stains Of mud, and the scent . Of all kinds of dirt, Seem never to hurt The beggars wno there frequent. Here they come smiling, Intent on beguiling, Now cringing and whining, At their hard fate repining, Stealthily peeping, . Close to you creeping, Muttering and moaning, Grunting and groaning, Drowsily droning, With endless refrain, Eager for,gain, Their greedy palms itching, Their long fingers twitching To snatch at the purses which money contain. There are beggav who claim Your help, as they're lame, !hi who, when they are at home, can dance all the same. There are beggars who've whined For years that they're blind, Yet, when they're not seen, their sight they soon find. There are beggars who sing Sankey's hymns, but who'll fling Loud oaths at your head if von don't ;ive anything. And when the day's over They'll revel in clover. Here's a canting old sinner Now eats a good dinner; That, boy begged for water, He now will pots of porter. And so every one Finds begging such fun, That, doubtless, while many an honest man starves, The beggar, in living, does nothing by halves.

"Yes, sir," responded the new boy, and then he hastened to wait upon an elderly female who wanted a stamp. "Anythin' else, mum ?" inquired the ambitious boy, politely. "Hair-dye, cosmetic, face powder, rheumatic drops, belladonna, molp destroyer—" The elderly female licked the stamp viciously and left the door open as she went ont. • Blanchar Jerrold's menviir of hi 3 father is full of admi-able anecdotes of the great wit. For instance, Douglas Jerro!tl regarded the adapter as somebody who • managed to cozen a reputation for originality from the foreigner. D scusaing one day with Mr. Planche this vexed quo s on, this gentleman insisted upon claiming some of his characters as strictly original creations. "Do you remember my Baroness in 'Ask no Questions?'" said Mr. Plariche. "Yes, indeed, I don't think I ever saw a piece of yours without being struck by your barren- ness," was the retort. This closed the discussion with a hearty latiets AN UNSEMEISII CITY ARAM—Lord Ashley (afterwards the Earl of Sha(tesbury). once told the House of Com- mons a touching story of the hardships of the "gutter children." Be knew a boy, hes said, who spent the greater part of his nights throughout the bitter winter of 1847 inside the iron roller of Regent's Park ! Every evening this lad used to climb over the railings, and creep into the curious shelter which he had found from the biting blast. And then Lord Ashley went on to show how kind the very poorest are to one another. So much comfort had the boy enjoyed in the roller that he resolved to give a less-fortunate chum a share of his home, promising to "let him into Ft good thing"—which he did in more serials than one. That waa real unselfish- ness'; was it not?—Little Folks Magazine. AVOIDABLE GRIFFS.—No one, at least no one who has lived as long as I have, ',mulct attempt to ignore the agonies of life; its bitter disappointments, its cruel losses, its sufferings of mind and body; griefs that come direct from God; and others, harder to bear, that seem to come through man, anguishes needless and avoidable. We all know them. Each one has his own burthen to carry; the only difference is how he carries it; whether it crushes him, that is, whether he allows it to crush him, or not. Therefore I hold, and I repeat it once more, that the worth of life lies in a man's own hands; and know- ing this, it is piteous to see the young throwing life away, wasting time, health, love. happiness, squandering madly all these blessings which will never return, and then accusing Providence of making life not worth living—The Aotlior of "John Halifax, Gentleman." TER ADVANCR OF SCOLPTIIRE IN THR PAST HALF'. CENTIIRY.—MR. GITSIERT.—Between the British sculptor and the British public there was a great gulf fixed, and neither party knew in the least how it could,ofshouldbe bridged. The sculptor went on producing his gods and his goddesses, and the British public said, "Very fine!" and passed on; he went on producing his busts, and the public scrutinised them for the likeness only. There was one field only on which one might have expected Sculptor and public to meet on something like common artistic ground. For monuinental sculpture, there was always a certain demand, and it gave scope for the ex- pression of genuine modern sentiment expressed in modern language. But the melancholy failures in St. Paul's and Westminster Abbey show how little our sculptors were capable of seizing the opportunity. Britannias like Minervas, with tridents; angels like nymphs, with trumpets; cherubs like Cupids. with wings and without bodies; canncns and coils of rope; tags and scrolls and clouds of marble—all the stage properties of both sculpture and painting gathered in olumsy profusion around a central figure—such were their modes of expressing national pride and private sorrow. . . . The Italians of the Renaissance were in much the same position as these sculptors of ours. They, too, were absorbed in the study of antique art, and had no other sculpture for a model. But they saw what the problem was, and they solved it. They never thought of adopting the spirit of classic art; they did not accept its dead ideal; they aspired after no already- attained perfection. They only studied it to gain its principles, and to find a way to express their own feelings in sculpturesque language. 'S'Even Niccola Pisan°, though IA took figures frankly from Roman bas-reliefs, used them to express his own thoughts, and was never less than original; and Donatello, the Della Bobbies, Ghiberti, Michelangelo, Quercia, and the rest of the illustrious group, made sculpture live again as freely and vigorously ' as it had ever lived in ancient Greece and Rome. From these sculptors our own might have learnt to be faithful, without being commonplace, to be tender without affectation, to be familiar without vulgarity, to be sub- lime without plagiarism; but it has remained, for the younger sculptors ot the present day to appreciate the examples they set us. Among these younger men none has appreciated it more than Mr. Alfred Gilbert Technically, he has achieved the power to do what he will; he is, at least, a master of his craft, whether as a worker in marble or metal. Interested in every branch of his profession, and desiring to express himself in every di- rection; prodigal of labour and invention, he has cer- tainly one of the most active and cultivated art-intelli- gences of the day, and must, in the nature of things, have much influence on the spirit and direction of the art of the present generation of 'Englishmen. It is, therefore, of no little interest to examine in what way this influence is likely to be exerted. That it has begun • already cannat be doubted. . . As far as the Royal Academy is concerned, their recognition of his merit is not surprising. They have, as a body, always treated sculptors with honour; and this has not been less the case under the present President of the Royal Academy —sir Frederick Leighton, himself one of the finest of living English sculptors. No recent elections at the Royal Academy have been received with more approval than those which have rapidly elevated Mr. Hamo Thornycroft to full honours, and bestowed the rank of Associate on Mr. Gilbert, Mr. Brock, and Mr. Onslow Fords—The JP gezine of Art for November.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

Beeenooe.—The summer has been too short for this crop to attain its usual weight, and many of the roots are not of a useable size, but, on the other hand, there are very few large coarse roots of the mangold wurtzel type. The roots cannot withstand sharp frosts, conse- quently they should be taken up and stored whore frost will not reach them, and they should have similar care in that way as is required for potatoes, only those are best kept quite dry, and the beet are best fairly moist, as if exposed to a dry atmosphere they are apt to shrivel. Our plan is to pack them in a shed in sand or ashes— that is, a layer of roots, then a layer of sand, and so on, and if the frost is keen, a few inches of stable litter are laid over the front and sides of the heap. To take up the roots, perhaps, the best implement is a fork,a,which , should be inserted in the ground at such a distance from the roots that there is no probability of injuring them. Roots that have the misfortune to be broken or lacer- ated are rendered almost useless, as they bleed, as gar- deners term the process of sap exudation, and the colour of the beet, when cooked, will be a pale dirty-red, instead of a beight crimson. It is possible to inpair the colour also by •over-boiling, and where that occirrs the roots are soft and flabby. A well-cooked beet should • have a certain amount of crispness, and the colour bright and tempting. Large roots take longer to boil than small ones, and it is always best tra drop roots of equal dimensions in the pan together. They may then be ex- pected to be ready to come out at the same time. Un- like the majority, or, we might say, all roots, the beet requires no peeling, nor even washing, before being I cooked, hut after they are boiled and cooked Sufficiently to handle, the skin may be readily moved with the finger and thumb.—Parsnipe : These are quite hardy, and will be left in the ground, except a few that will be taken up shortly in case of the ground becoming frozen so hard as to prevent them being dug when required. TM? FRONT GARDETC—We have not yet taken up our dahlias, but intend doing so the first fine day, so that the roots may be freed of as much moisture as possible before they are packed in their winter quarters. Each root should have a label attached,-with the name or the colour of the variety written upon it, which will be some guide for the disposal ot the colours at planting time; and if a few plants die in the winter, as usually happens, the deficiency can be made up by striking cut- tings or dividing the roots, if there are any representa- tives of the defunct ones. Sorts that have proved them- selves bad winterers should have special care taken of them by placing them in a box by themselves, or singly in pots, with dry sand round the roots. They must be examined occasionally daring the winter, and if there are signs of decay the plants may be saved if the de- cayed • portions are removed.—The Tulip: The second week, or not later than the third week, in this month is looked up by florists as the latest date at which the Tulip may be planted. The Tulips of the florist are usually planted in beds where they can be protected when in flower by constructing a skeleton frame over them to support a canvass on a roller, which may be moved up and down as required. An acquaintance who grew them for exhibition planted in 4-foot beds, six inches distant every way, which made seven rows across the bed, and arranged therm so that two of a class did not come together, whatever the length of the bed might be. Before planting, three inches of the surface of the bed was thrown out on either side, and then left, made even with the rake, and the rows marked by stretching the line along and pressing it gently the whole of its length with the back of the spade so as to make a mark; and in the same way the cross rows were marked, which left the whole bed in squares of six inches, a bulb being de- posited where the lines croSsed, and gently pressed half their depth into the soil, and then covered over with the three inches of soil thrown out at the commencement. 1 The beds thus planted wilt need no further attention ' until May, when the flowers must be well shaded from the sun, which spoils the colours for exhibition purposes. TEE GRRENROCSE.—Pot Roses: Those, plants already established in pots should be turned out, and the worn- out soil moved away from the roots with a pointed stick until the ball is re luced to two inches all round, which will admit of the plant being placed back in a similar-sized pot to the one it has occupied with a two- inch lining of soil round the roots. Fibry loam with one-sixth of decayed manure and a handful of bone meal is a good compost for pot roses. Plants !growing in the open ground may be taken up now and potted in the same mixture; and if taken into the greenhouse about Christmas they will he in flower about April or May, according to the temperature kept up in the struc- ture. They must not be pruned until they have started to grow, and then we only advise the removal of weakly growth and taking off the weak points of long shoots, the portion left of these being tied down. ae-t.teM!

"One leg ts shorter than the other. and he limps. Now, what would you do in such a case?" "I think I should limp, too." " I will bet you a new hat," said a gentleman friend, "that you will come down out of that chair before I ask 'cot twice." "Done)." replied his friend. "Come -down," cried the other. "I will not," said his friend, with much obstinacy. "Then stop till I ask you a second time," said the other. Perceiving that he never would be asked a second time, the gentleman in the chair came down in a double sense.

Flume, Smith, and other literati of the last century used to frequent a tavern in a low street in Edinburgh called the Potter-row, where, if their accommodations were not of the Erst order, they had at least no scanti- ness of their victuals. One day, as the landlady was bringing in a third supply of some particularly good dish. she addressed them thus •—" They ca' ye the literawti, I believe; oct if they were to ca' ye the eater- crwti, they would be nearer the mark I" EMBROIDERING BOOBS. Among the arts wherewith high-born dames during the ages of chivalry were wont to while away the tedium of their lives, few were more useful, and none more beauti7ul, than that of embroider- ing book covers. There are not many mettival remains that bring home to us the terrible dulness and monotony .of the lives of the noble women of olden days so forcibly as the immense pieces of tapestry which still line the walls of some of our old baronial and manorial real. dences. Many must have taken years of labour to coin-- plete, and there is reason to believe that, for every one finished, scores were commenced and flung aside from very weariness before they were half done. Embroider- ing a book cover had all the advantages, and none of the drawbacks, of working a tapestry; the most elabo- rate folio offered some vista of completion, whereas such a hanging as that which covers some thirty square, yards of St. Mary's Hall at Coventry—in the writer's opinion, the most magnificent of our medival tapes- tries—meant long, years oiNuninteresting labour. Yet, for every embroidered book remaining, there are at least half a dozen pieces of tapestry. The reasons are obvious. Whereas every residence offered a plethora of bare walls, the books to cover were very few indeed. Tapestry almost any one could work when once the design was drawn, but a cover demanded a much greater amount of care, skill, and neatness, a more correct eye, and higher artistic temperament. The materials for the one too, were much easier to obtain than for the other; and so it came to pass that while many high-born dames worked tapestry, few, outside the walls of convents, had the opportunity of doing the more delicate and pleasant work. There is sufficient evidence to show that in the cloister it was not an uncommen employment for the nuns' spare hours, and, no doubt, the choirs of nearly every collegiate church once blazed with the gorgeous bindings of its service-books..,—The Woman's World. With due apologies to the 1. reader (if reader there be), net for the lengthy qte. tions, which we hope will have IcKmin not without interest but for the intervening remarks, not only lengthy, but also we fear tedious (when not faulty in other and more serious respects)—with such qtaalified apology, let us conclude by a quotation once more from Mr. Kingsley's able and eloquent pamphlet. "A true nationalky, founded on . and combining thoroughly the free indi- vidual manhood of a country, is as irresistible as a force of nature. High statesmanship will recognise in it a political factor of paramount importance. To the infinite credit of Mr. Gladstone he has. fishy comprehended the truth that "magnanimity in politics, is ant seldom the truest wisdom" and that nothing is more essential to the discussion of Irish affairs than !generous sentiments, compassionate sympathies, and noble and elevated , thoughts.' He has fully justified and fulfilled the !prophecy of a farmer ally "—(the reader can hardy fail to recognise whose.) "I say that the man who, lead- the counsels of the Queee's Government, shall grasp this great question and conclude it, will do that which in future time the pen of history will delight to trace. He will, to the very full, gratify the noblest ambition of his mind, and he will build up for himself a lasting memorial in the happiness and thegratitude of a regener- ated nation." .111.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOV
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOV
FURTHER (AND FOR THE PRESENT • FINAL) NOTES AND QUERIES ON SOME OBJECTIONS TO HOME RULE. BY "Holm RULE."

And now we ore to what has been perhaps the most serious difficulty of the whole question; that of rear. ing the actual and portentious existence of Irish National aspirations. Home Rule is:objected to because,as people tell us, the Irish do not want it. What they want, says one. "Is the land": Says another, "Catholic supre- macy": Another something else—anything except the reality—; but, in most eases, their aspirations are said to consist essentially, if not solely, of a desire to secure for themselves the land. A simple affirmation to the contrary, by way of reply,if coming from a quarter in which there maybe supposed to exist a bias in favour of Home Rule, would hardly herebe sufficient to carrymuch weight with fair and open minded Home Rulers, to say nothing of Unionists. W. shall therefore again fall back upon Mr. Goldwin Smith as our authority. The last quotation was from his writings in 1861. The following were his opinions six years later, at the time of the Fenian insur- rection: an insurrection analagous to the more constitu- tional and less desperate, though more comprehensive, agitation of the last decade. He says ;

The Fenian movement is not religious, nor radically economical (though no doubt it has in it a socialistic element) but national, and the remedy for it must be one which cures national discontent. This is the great truth which the Idnglish people have to lay to heart. Mr. Goldwin Smith then dispels the notion that the Irish question is-a religious one. When Peniaaism first appeared, the Orangenien, in aCcord- ance with their fixed idea, ascribed it to the priests. They were undeceived, I was told, by seeing a priest run away from the Fenians in fear of his life. Neither was it a question of the land. . . " "
The laud question, no doubt, lies nearer to the heart a the matter, and it is the great key to the Irish history in the past; but I do not believe that even this Is fundamental. . . . .
He then states what is "fundamental."

The real root of the disaffection which exhibits itself at pre- sent in the guise of Fenianism, and which has been suddenly kindled into flame by the arming of the Irish in the American Civil War, but which existed before in a nameless and smouldering state, is, as I believe, the want of national insti- tutions, of a national capital, of any objects of national reverence and attachment, and conseqently of anything deserving to be called national life. _ . .

It ma; be possible to illustrate, aid bring home to the mind, the full force and magnitude of these national aspirations by comparing them with the only other sentiment which is equally and more than equally deep seated and wide spread. We believe there is no impro- priety in drawing a comparison between the spirit of nationalism and that of religion. • . . . .

Of the spiritual forces 'Cvhich have influenced the world's history, probably not even patriotism, in all its varied forms, has exercised over the feelings of mankind a sway anything like so great as its lofty cohabitant 'of the mind, religion. The immense controlling, guiding, and fortifying power which this exerts over the whole human race, civilized and uncivilized, will not be dis- puted. Upon what is this influence founded? Let us take the religion, not of sOrne tribe as yei unemerged from barbarism (we know the influence which religion in the shape of superstition, or vice versa, has over them), but of Europe, America, England if you will, and see wherein its power lies. The various creeds into which that section of the world which calls itself Christian is divided are composed of multifarious beliefs, some of greater, some of lessor importance. Leaving out of con- sideration the latter, and referring only to the funda- mental doctrines upon which the whole of the religious edifice, at once elaborate and solid, may be said to be based,—we ask, can the truth of them be logically and conclusively demonstrated? The answer is that while some admit of proof, or partial proof, others, of import- ance to its stability, are incapable either of proof or disproof, or require the acceptance as fact, not alone of the uncertain, but of the positively inconceivable and unthinkable.

A.—To take the most important example ; —the popular conception of the nature and powers of the Deity is, as cannot be denied, but a pseud-concept, and in reality unthinkable. We are not here expressing any opinion upon the amount of truth or error, which, on the average, may pervade the Protestant religion' or any religion. The point we emphasise is this. That of the numerous creeds which come under the bread denominations, Protestant and Catholic, many of the doctrines which go to form them, and upon which, not indeed the essential element of truth, but still the exist- ence of the numerous creeds of to-day, in their present form, or as at present understood and accepted,—that many of these doctrines involve in the human mind flat contradictions of thought. Yet men's faith in them has been so strong that, rather than abandon them, they have sacrificed their lives. What is the explanation? It is that these doctrines—not perhaps alone, but mainly and in the last resort—have their foundations in the heart rather than the brain. It is as F. W. Robert- son says, that "there is something stronger than reason, more powerful than logic, viz., belief." A per- son, because he cannot prove conclusively by ordinary logic, by logic of argument, the truth of Christian faith, or the existence of a personal and partially compre- hensible First Cause, may become an agnostic or possibly refuse to believe in either. But blind and bigoted indeed must be the Atheist or agnostic who denies the immense amount of good, of help, and of comfort derived by individuals, as by nations, from the religion in which, though incapable of. logical proof, they have placed an undying hope and belief. The case of patriotism is analogous. people who claim the right to believe in that which it is yet impossible to prove, should not lightly deny the existence of nationalism and patriotism simply because their eyes are too dim to se. these impalpable essences. Nor if they do comprehend and realize the existence of a nationalist sentiment, should they be the ones to refuse to gratify it because they think it unreasonable. May not its indulgence be, in some degree at least, to the disheartened and distressed Irish, a feeling, a natural instinct, call it what you will, but something to take them out of themselves; some- thing to raise their minds for a time above the wearying troubles and difficulties of their daily life, to fill them with inspiring thoughts for the future, in place of many a bitter recollection of the past. May it' not, directly and indirectly, help, comfort, elevate and fortify them. It were not therefore to be sneered at, even supposing it should be (which it is not) incapable of logical demonstra- tion, and to some minds unreasonable. We assert that It is not unreasonable. For in one important respect the element of Irish nationalism does differ from that Of religion with which we have ventured to compare it. , We have discussed at some length the causes which have chiefly led to the present condition of poverty, and often of extreme wretchedness, best described by the French expression la misers. We have seen how their industries were nipped in the bud and ruined, and how, by the saMie power, it was attempted by the penal laws, "to debase, in them, human nature itself." We know who enforced the laws that enabled the absentee landlords to carry on their system of "legalized oppression." sucking out, so to gpe,ak, the very blood of the country. Has this no bearing upon Irish sentiment, and upon the direction, the form which it has taken? The moving linger writes, and, having writ, Moves on, nor all your piety nor wit Can lure it back to cancel half a line, Nor all your tears wipe out one word of it. Has not oppression deepened and intensified the feelings of " a peasantry characterized by an attachment to the Fatherland unparalled among the people of any country known to history ?"* May not an Irishman say to himself, under our own Parliament of 1782, had it not been abolished, had we not been foully robbed of it, these things would not have come to pass; they would have been impossible. 'Then if you have kindly feeling towards us, restore it to us. Yes, in this important respect there is a difference between the belief in Home Rule and that in religion. Both spring from the heart, but the former has stern unsentimental logic and reason, has the mind on its side also. Without entering into a discussion of the several advantages which directly and indirectly Ireland will obtain shortly after the granting of Home Rule, it is plain to every Irishman that a Parlia- ment in Dublin will have more time to look after his interests than the one at Westminster. He knows well hew unlikely it is that reforms will be then, as hitherto they always have been, "too late," resisted and delayed by a Tory party, and an Upper House of which the majority form a permanent obstruction. That not having the same anti-Irish feeling and the same general ignorance (comparatively speaking) of Irish affairs to , contend with, those affairs will be more judiciously as , well as more promptly settled. Further, and whether he would express it in the same exact words or not, the Irishman instinctively or unconsciously apprehends and feels the truth enunciated by an able exponent of I nationalism when he wrote that "countries duly limited in extent, and compact in character, best serve to create and nurture to full strength a real sense of the words involved in the manifold relations of citizenship, and thereby contribute most effectively to the moral enlightenment and spiritual regeneration of the world.t And this, in fact, is the primary function which, in the purposes of nature, they were constituted to die- charge ;" also of the following :—" Hearts and heads ani- mated by devotion to the same environment soon come to understand the relations which ought to subsist between them; and social ties become consolidated when the permanent seat of their formation—the common country—inspires.the souls of the people with a passion- ate attachment." t This one fact, at least, is not to be ignored. All who have had the least chance of knowing, and excepting only those in whom the wish, is father to a contrary opinion, have given their testimony in support of what, taken as a whole, is irrefragable evidence of its truth. t And this fact, thus proved, is the existence of those ,national aspirations by which Ireland. years ago. "Came fairly into line with the other discontented nationalities of Europe." However you may deal with, you cannot everlastingly ignore them. And it becomes always

more pressing, that question, how shall we deal with ' them? Shall it be conciliation or coercion? Mr. Bull willhave to decide. There is little doubt now what that stalwart individual, freedom's tower of strength, will do whoa he has another opportunity of expressing his opinion; when the time comes again for him, after ample consideration, to make up his mind and pronounce his fiat—for peace or war, for good Or evil. He may ' determine 'to crush these nationalist sentiments and aspirations: in which attempt even Mr. Bull will not be wholly (if 'at all) successful. But while failing to extinguish the Promethean spark of patriotism he may, indeed, break the heart and almost put out thefiickering flame of vitality that remains in the people. For Ireland is a poor country in more ways than one. Energy and strength are wealth in a nation, and in these, Ire- land, from causes, some of which we have considered, is at present sadly deficient. Too often has chronic suffer- ing turned to deadly misery,nor has the spectre of famine walkedthe land without casting its shadow, and leaving its grey mark upon people as well as country. Also have famine and emigration, during the last 70 years, reduced the population from something under eight millions to ' something under five. Emigration has, it is said, been carrying off a yearly average of 80,000 inhabitants, generally the most enterprising and able bodied persons in the land.*

Thus has Ireland's vitality been sapped, and a blow ' from Mr. Bull's heavy hand would now tell severely upon her. So that, while failing, as aforesaid, to destroy Ireland's nationality, he -would undoubtedly be able to reduce to a lower ebb her vitality and nerve power whereby, harrassed and exhausted, she might reach ultimately to a state Of stagnant existence like to that of the Chinese. Do any of us desire such a thing? If not, let her be saved from the miseries of continued though suppressed revolution. Stagnation Mr. Buckle refers to in his history of civilization When he says—" of all evils, torpor is the most deadly : give us paradox, give us error, give us what .you.will so that you save us from stagnation." How far a high handed policy of "taming and commanding the Irish" would be attended with success of this kind, may be a matter of opinion, but it would have the certain effect of throwing back again into the "slow, sullen furnace of mute hatred, suspicion and discontent," two nations intended to live otherwise on terms of mutual regard, confidence and respect. This course of action, with such attendant consequence, Mr. Bull may take if guided by selfish class bigotry, which respects no nationalism except the worst fiorm of its own; or if he listens to the promptings of a false and r unworthy spirit of dominatory pride and prejudice. But he may do otherwise. Nay, dismissing all such invidious suggestions, shall we not roundly assert that he will do far otherwise? As one of the greatest sages of this century says (after rallying Mr. Bull for his dullness) : "His inner silent feeling of what is true, what does agree with fact, what is doable and what is not doable—this seeks its fellow in the world. .. . . . Nay withal, stupid as he is, our dear , John—ever after infinite tumblings and spoken platitudes innumerable from barrel- heads and Parliament - benches—he does settle down somewhere about the just conclusion; you are certain that his jmnblings and tumblings will end, after years or.centuries, in a stable equilibrium:l The English people are at last getting to the bottom of this question, and the Irish may have faith in their settling down somewhere about the just conclusion. 'rMr. Bull, for instance, begins to see thatr there is something radically wrong in the policy under which it is necessary to lock up, whose only success consists in locking up, the most patriotic of Ireland's citizens. While the unruliness of Irish aeitatione and insurrections is violently decried, h e—law-alltding, law-respecting citizen as he is—knows bhat "approximate justice will strive to accomplish itself; if not in one way, then in another." His consti- tution, his laws, his executive—these he greatly respects, for they suit hire. They are the work of his own hand, and besides a natural feeling of affection for them as such, he is interested in seeing that they are upheld. Were if otherwise, would he regard them with equal respect and affection? He would not. "For the gowns of learned serjeants are good; parchment records, fixed forms, and poor terrestrial Justice, with or without horsehair-what sane man will not reverence these ?" And yet, to continue the quotations, "Behold, the man is not sane but insane, who coasiders these ahem as venerable. Oceans of horsehair, continents of parchment, and learned-serjeant eloquence, were it continue .1 till the learned tongue wore itself, small in the indefatigable learned mouth, cannot make unjust, just. The grand question still remains, was the judgment just? If un- just, it will not and cannot get harbour for itself or con- • tinue to have, footing in the Universe,whichwas made by other than one Unjust. Enforce it by never such statut- ing. three readings, royal assents; blow it to the four winds with all manner of quilted trumpeters and pur- suivants, in the rear of them, never so many gibbets and hangmen, it will not stand—it cannot stand. From all souls of men, from all ends of nature, from the throne of God abeve, there are voices bidding it away, away! Does it take no, warning, does it stand strong in its three readings, in its gibbets and artillery-parks? The more woe is to it, the frightfuler Vroe. It will continue stand ing for-its day, for its year, for its century, doing evil all the while; but it has One enemy who is Almighty' dis- solution, explosion, and the everlasting laws of nature incessantly advance towards it; and the deeper its root- ing, more obstinate its continuing, the deeper also and huger will its ruin and overturn be." Are not these eloquent passages applicable to the,lril.' question? Not less so, we believe; than the, following delivered by Lord Chatham, in reference to the great rebellion herein already mentioned. Said Lord Chatham :
"There was ambition, there was violence, there was sedition; but no man shall persuade me that it was not the cause of liberty on •one side and tyranny on the other."t

Of those who think that our first duty or business, as regards Irishmen, is to tarne and command them, some will remain unconvinced, chiefly those who are not open to conviction either by fact or logic. Such would fain have us follow in the footsteps of those whose object was, for so long a time—simply that of making Ireland finglish. In the footsteps of that "committee 'of the English Parliament" composed of "Protestants of the old gromwellian Puritan breed, who could do the work of goading to perfection—men who, having become recreant to the principles of a regenerative and liberty-loving faith, were brutalized by bigotry and dehumanized by-the use of remorseless power.' For- tunately the majority of the British people sternly decline to follow in those footsteps. Astute politicians may expatiate upon the difficulties and obstacles that are to be encountered in carrying out the policy of the Liberal party. It is of no avail. Mr. Bull remembers the objections, the difficulties, the obstacles which were raised to other reforms that, nevertheless, were passed, and by which, spite of doleful predictions to the con- trary, he has greatly benefitted. He sees and acknow- ledges some, at any rate, of the difficulties pointed out to him, but he is of opinion that they can begot over ; that they need not and must not and will not be allowed to stand in the way of a settlement at which it is to the interests of both nations to arrive, and which is ' on that account, and on other perhaps higher grOunds, desired by both. Our well disposed but unfortunate friend, the politician who deals in narrow logic to the e.reltenon of that high property of the mind, imagination, will hold to it that some modicum of material assist- ance is all that is called for in this difficulty ; for he is unable to grasp that part of it which is immaterial and Is bound therefore to obtain a false conception of the whole. He forgets, in short, that" soul is not synony• mous with stomach."

That the establishing of self-government, of popular government, in Ireland, is required in the interests of civilization as of humanity and justice ; that it will, therefore jn the long run, be advantageous not , only to Ireland but to Britain also and the rest of the civilized world—this may not be a 'mater of absolute certainty. What in human affairs is so? /tut it is morn than probable ; and probability, as Burke says, must be our guide. This has been a difficult questiom for Mr. Bull to decide, but he has been slowly making up his mind not only to follow the advice which Mr. Bright is said to have once given to a political friend in a similar state of uncertainty—by" taking the generous side?!; but to adopt a course that shall be in conformity and harmonize with the truth which still asserts itself is contained in such great maxims as these following. Every civilized country is entitled to settle its internal affairs in its own way,4and no other country ought to interfere with its discretion ' • because one country, even with the best intentions, has no chance of properly understanding the internal affairs of another. §

And • - "The rules of politics," it has been eloquently said, " are eternal, because they repose oh morality ; and there are no politics true, efficacious, fruitful, when force violates, even momentarily and temporarily, the eternal principles of justice and humanity." Besides those who fail in, or who take a pride in discarding imagination, what they call fanciful and absurd sentiment, but who recognise evils to be got rid of somehow, there are others, shallow and thoughtless politicians who, with characteristic levity, will tell him that the Parliament at Westminster does or must do for Ireland just as well as for England (presumably because they think so) and that no reasonable Irishman can wish for a different form of government. But history tells another tale and it is none the less true, as Mill says, that "the capability, of any people for fulfilling any given form of government, cannot be pronounced on by any sweeping rule. Knowledge of the particular people, and general practical judgment and sagacity, must be the guides." It is now high time that we should recollect imposed limitations of time and space which the reader might fear had been well nigh forgotten: Wei therefore bring these protracted, though all too incomplete

, CHAPTER XXL SCREWED UP. These young rascals took a boisterous delight in the thought that they were going to assume the novel and fascinating rge of :supporters of law and order. To combine this with an 'artistic piece of rowdyism, seemed to them a highly humorous thing. And humorous it was, if, as Sydney Smith says, humour in its truest form is the discovery of a con- gruity between the apparently most 'incongruous things.l ,As soon as..the plan had been formed they proceeded to tarry it out. They swarmed up to Raymond's rooms and found him snoring—for wine is a strong soporific. The screws and screw-driver were found lying on the table. They first locked Raymond's bedroom' door and confiscated the key. Then they 19cked the door of his sitting-room, also conlAeating the key, and fluiaily seresved:up the outer eak and removed the heads of the screws with a dia. belie care worthy of a better cause. Thus Raymond was triply secured—" sealed as tight as an entombed dervish," as one of these " moonlighters" remarked. But they were not satisfied. So they wrote in large letters on the outside of his oak, Not to be unfastened; screwed by order of the dean.—E. SMITH (dean) ;" carried the keys into the backyard, where they buried them in a rubbish heap, and then hurried off to bed with roars of laughter. Of course the dean's authority is supreme over the scouts, and so when Raymond's scout came next morning early and found the notice on the oak, he did not dare to remove it. He went about his other work till lunch time, and left Raymond hermetrically sealed. _ _

Meanwhile the unhappy youth slept till late, and .yroke about 11 o'clock with a burning headache —the " Katzenjammer " as the Germans call it. As he slowly gained consciousness all the events of the former night came back to him with that heavy weight of agony which the Morning brings. He remembered that he had disgraced himself—that he would never be able to lift up his head again in the college—that the only friends he had would now cast him off. As he realised all this the complexity of feelings—shame, self-reproach, remorse, combined with that conviction of martyrdom and injury common to every weak mind when suffering by cause of its own weakness—overcame him entirely in an overwhelming sense of misery, and he buried his, head in his bedclothes and wept. ' But after a time be pulled himself together and slowly dressed. Raymond was as weak in body as in mind, and could not stand dissipation like his stronger friends. This morning his fast,growing weakness had been brought to a climax by the scene of last night. He had a burning fever and racking headache. He did not know it himself at the time, but the grip of a long illness was already fast upon him. He dressed defiantly, but he often had to rest in the middle—dropping back upon his bed faint and sick. ' At last he was dressed, and put his hand to the , door, intending to pass into his sitting-room. Horror of horrors lit was locked on the outside. He looked out of the window. It was too high either for a leap or a ladder. All the stories he had heard rushed back upon him. He was "screwed up I He put his head out of his bedroom 'window and, shouted. But this window looked over an empty yard. There was no chance of anyone hearing. He battered the door in impotent wrath. It was use-, less. - • Half an hour's battering brought no one. Finally, tired out with fever, shouting, and hunger, he fell back on his bed and lost consciousness. • Meanivhile, the scout's slow suspicions had been gradually roused. It was not ordinary for ,the dean to screw up • young gentlemen. He surely, at any rate, did not mean to starve him out. He wa4 anew - scout that, term, or he would have perceived the ruse in a moment. But at last he went timidly to the dean and asked him when he might unscrew the young gentleman! The good man was overcome with horror at the idea of .his "screwing up" anyone—a practice which he him- self had never on any occasion omitted to de- nounce I You might as well accuse an Irish land-- lord of moonlighting, an alderman of revolutianary tendencies, or a capitalist of rioting in Wall 'Mall. The scout told him that he had found a notice to that effect on the gentleman's door. " A scandalous forgery !" exclaimed the offended don; "whoever forged my name shall be sent down immediately. We will have no insubordination here! Unscrew the young gentleman immediately, and bring me the names of those.who hare scr6ved him up !" It was easier said than done. Two carpenters laboured at the door for two hours before the last headless screw was removed. The oak was destroyed, and then another difficulty occurred. Where were theikeys ? After a long search, one of the fast set took compassion and sent an anonymous note to the scout telling him where to lookfor them. After long diggink they were rescued from the rubbish heap: At last, at 4 o'clock in the afternoon, Raymond's bedroom ' door was thrown open arid the last barrier removed. , Everyone concerned had long wondered at the passivity of the young man. Most people howl at windows on such occasions, but no shouting in the I yard under Raymond's window could draw a Sound. Rumour went about that he had been murdered, or that he had escaped in the night like St. Paul, "by the wall." Nor were they reassured when, on open- ing the door, they found him unconscious on the bed. He was picked up and restored to consciousness by cold water and brandy ; but was soon in a raging feyer. They put him to bed and sent for the doctor. When Fielding heard that he was ill he came at *nee to his assistance, and was so slarmedat his symptoms that he thought it better to send for Ursula,
CHAPTER XXII. -NWN.
SENT DO'

Meanwhile Ursula had been happier than before at S. Agatha. For her brother's sake and the well-being of the villagers round her, she would willingly have impoverished her.elf, findin g no joy like the joy of self- forgetfulness, the losing of one's self in the happiness of another. Raymond would have complained that the house was deadly dull with an absence of guests—. an absence of conversation. But 'Ursula', with her natural love of ecenery, found an undeniable fascina- tion in pastoral life, and now that she was happier about her brother,whom she believed to be thoroughly under Fielding's influence, it was easier for her to find her resources in home pursuits. ,So little did she know of the change which had really taken place in Ray,that she still persisted in lookincr upon him as a lad of shrinking nerve and snper-sensitive delicacy. Re had improved greatly during the six weeks he spent with Fielding on the Continent, and though on his return to S. tgatha he had instantly relapsed into that mild languor which 'Seemed to be in .keeping with Ursula's belief in slow evolution,he was so handsome, so charming to women, with the pathetic expression of the violet,blackdashed almond-shaped eyes, that one could believe no evil of him, and was instinctively reminded of, "Narcissus is the glory able race, For who does nothing with a better grace r If he spent four months in the year in amusing lajm- ' self, Ursula' remincledlerself that at least six months would be devoted to learned pursuits. _ . .

.• The easy philosophy of Horace is as common now as in his time, and Ray,on reading him,had instantly declared his intention of adopting Horace's philosophy is that most suited to the world he lived in. He and Ursula had had some hot arguments about it, but she comforted herself, by reflecting that after all he might set out for his Oxford life with a wore system of ethics. To bear what comes,'not expect too much—care little abont anyone, not be earnest enough to quarrel, not take the trouble to admire ; if Raymond really could adopt it it might save him from some of the temptations which his sister had most dreaded for him. It was not the highest ideal, but it was perhaps good for a sensitive nature, and strength and energy might be prophesied to come ! unexpectedlyto one who determined not to be daunted by trifles. 1 So thought the sallguine sister, reconciling herself to the "masterly inactivity" into which Ray had sub- Sided as scion as he had passed his "metric." ' She w 6 not alarmed by !As letters, though with a shrewder perception of character she might •have read between the liues,and have feared that Ray .was becoming too familiar with. the whist-set,and was . suddenly, beginning to understand English billiards. Like Dr. Havard before him Fielding had expos- , hulated with Ursula or . her imprudence in supplying ter brother with too much money. He spoke with the candour which nialies a man disliked, and Utsula felt inclinettto answer, "Some people would call it open-hearted, not ex- travagant." "So long as he isn't lazy all will be well,' answered the young tutor. • "He'd like to grab me by the arm and make me work like a slave,hut there is really no occasion to do

omen a villainous heap ot work," wrote .Kaymond tO his sister after his first week. And Ursula, who was not a good diplomatist,and who scarcely understood how illiudged were her en- comiums of Fielding, causing her brother to remove himself by imperceptible degrees from his influence, bad no conception of the sort of scrape into whieb Rayinond• had, fallen, When she -reaa the letter in Which an .attenrpt:was made to break the truth to her by delicate hints. , Even when Fielding met her at the Oxford station she was still almost completely in the dark. She vaguely took in that they had associated with those sort of fellows who believed in neither angel nor devil, and who would not ,put out a hand to arrest anyone who was inclined by nature to take the down' ward path. But all this conveyed no meaning to her. And when Fielding went on to speak a little mere plainly she did not understand what charge he could be making—his words were like the dull roar ,of vehicles in her ears. "Sent, down ! Only that he had not been in a fit state to be moved.' She winced and pulled herself together when he tried to explain the ,reason.., She half understood that the terror had come upon her in a new form which shehad always dreaded for Raymond—and, of course —for herself. Was she not 'nixed up with all her brother's ill-doing? Did she wish to claim a separate identity superior to his? .No, now that the spectre was facing her she would make a ,brave stand against It. Her heart rose up against Fielding;, she was Ore he was too severe; he could not possibly comprehend what a charge lie was making ! The charge Aves, not unintelligible. She could not pretend that h• was strange to hey. Yet for Raymond's sake s,he smiled a superior smile, "Ali, you do not know--' " I am afraid 1 do," he answered, boggling 1" speech, and hemming like a country lout, as he tried to explain how the University would never be a fitting place for her brother. Hid serious manner chilled her, and she herself was inconsistent—in the one moment pretending that the offence Was but small thing to assuMe such disproportionate impor" tance, and, in the next, shrinking back with loapk; ing from all mention of it,, in her young, untrieu virtue, ready to empty the vials of her wrath on it, if not on the offender. "Many Men of his sort are wanting in strong fibre," she said, in a strange forced voice, turning oe her informer.

"I don't think you ought always to excuse a man for weakness," he answered gravely, having by thie time recovered his usual self,control. "Those wh° care for him would not ad Mit it. There are great po" sibilities of good in him—there always were—the finer qualities side by side with the baser ones." , He spoke in a pitying voice, but she resented grain of pity. Ile was contrasting her with hez brother—the one enerp.etic,the other languid, the one stirring inaction and full of presence of mind, the other dreamy and swayed by sudden passionate impulse; the one able to control herself, even such emergencies, the other wild and untameable when he attempted to assert himself—the one indif' ferent to the good opinion of others; the other with nothing virile in his hankering after being liked ; the one independent of luxury, ready to endure hardness, the other with too many artificial wants, too reanY finikin tastes. . Her voice sank very low, and quivered as if would break altogether; but still she pleaded against her better judgment—" A man like that, with a weak head, can drink himself into a (Flce! state in a very short time." He did not answer her; his very Dity kept hi,T silent. He had tried scathing sarcasm ilpon Rayme" but he had no words now. Nothing was heard but the rumbling of the cab which he had taken at the station to bnng her to her brother's rooms in college' When they reached their destination he let l‘ire' Wilson help her to alight. Louis Grandet would hay° overwhelmed her with officious- handiness whiell would have been almost burdensome, and voila probably have said with heat, "I believe, you for no one but your brother." But though the same thought crossed Fielding'S mind, and though '?„'" would have given worlds to say to her, "Any IST which falls on you must fall on me besides, °- stood aloof, watching his opportunity for the On° when he could ba of use.

REPUBLICANS "ASK FOR LORD SACK- VILLE BACK AGAIN." —hits York herald says it has the highest authority the statement that an effort is being made to secure reappointment of Lord Sackville as Minister to the ted States when the Harrison Administration comes power. The arguments in favour of the movement that the Minister was sacrificed to meet a political -^v, that the magnitude of the offence was exag- by reason of political conditions at the time, that the judgment of the American people after the `shall have been dispassionately looked at will be able to his reappointment. Lord Sackville has powerful Republican friends who think this a . opportunity to snub President Cleveland, whom 'they seem unable to forgive for keeping them out of 130tVer for four years. THE NEW VICEROY OF INDIA. Barsmst, MONDAY MORNINO.—The Marquis and Mar- chioness of Lansdowne, who had arrived by the over- land route from Calais, have left this port, on board the 'Peninsular and Oriental Company's steamer Sutley, ea ?WU for India. An important -announcement with regard to the de- ?epees of India was made by Lord Dufferin on Saturday Patialia. The Imperial Government will not accept raoney in aid .of military expenditure, but it will enter into arrangements by which the native warlike races %Elbe employed in the defence of India against a foreign invader. British officers will lead and instruct thes, levies, who will be supplied with modern rifles and cannon. In this way the forces at the disposal of the Calcutta Government will be enormously strengthened. STRANGE CONFESSION OF MURDERS. Much local interest has been aroused in Vienna by the arrest of a man who committed two cruel murders ten Yenrsego. The victims were an innkeeper and his wife, who were found dead one rnornine without any clue to the perpetrator of the crime being found. No suspicion was attached to the man and -woman servant, who Passed the night out of the house. On Friday the mar,- servant, now a thriving milkmen, beat his housekeep,r 40 baaly that she had to be 'taken to a hospital. Th, dressing of the wounds so painful that she was induced by it to reveal time story of the murcicc, where- aPottber master was arrested.

ATTEMPITRDAIIRDER INITHITECHAPEL. On Wednesday :treat excitement was caused iin the East End :and throughout the metropolis generally by the 'attempted murder of a woman in the district of the -recent tragedies. The crime was Committed within three minutes walk of Dorset- it, the eeene of thdiast murder,: and by a singular coincidence themictim of the George Yard murder lodged at the same houseaiad the woman murdered in Osborne- at. lived next-door. ' The circumstances therefore gave colourto the theory that the man who had committed the Crime was the individual known ag Jack the Ripper. The woman who was-• the victim of it-ednesday's outrage is named Annie Farmer. She is stated to be a marnied 'woman, of good appearance, and about 34 years of age. A woman who intimated that she had some knowledgenf the circumstances said the injured woman, who is also known as Matilda, has beers in thdhabit of lodging in common lodging houses .in the locality,and has known the • Wan who attacked dinsfor about twelve months. About seven o'clock onWeduesday morning-she met him near Spitalftelds Chroch, and told him that she was not able to pay for a bed. ',Theeman thereupon accompanied her tO 19, George-st. About half-past nine the man hurriedly left the bouse,.and almost immediately after-. Wards the woman camexiownstairs with her throat cut and bleeding profusely.. It appears that when the man attempted to cut her throat a struggle,ensued, and she. was able to give an alarm. Iler assailant then fled, and Was observed to leave the house, but the man who saw him attached no importance to the circumstance. Others, however, .who heard the alarm,followed, but lost. hira in the direction of ;Beneage-st. The woman says She can identify: him, and the police have circulated the following description "Wanted, for attempted murder on the 211.5 t inst., a anan, raged 36, height :sft. Bin., cent- Plexion dark, no whiskers, dark motastache ; dress; black jacket, vest, and trousers, and round black felt hat. Respectable appearance. Can be identified." Farmer was taken away by the police to the Police Station on .a stretcher, and that gave rise to the statement that she had been murdered; but it appears that the wound, although it bled freely, is only superficial, and noKlauger is apprehended. A large force of detectives was immetia,ely draftedto the dis- trict, and prosecuted inouiries throughout the day, but up to six in the evening the ,nivi had not been arrested. Several statements have been made to the authorities, but they do not accord with the description of the man Who is supposed to have eominitted the series oftmurders, and the general opinion, as well as that of the police, is that the author of Wednesdctis outrage is ;not the

inurderer in the previous cases. Farmer was removed from •Carnmereial-street police station in the afternoon to Whitechapel Infirmary. She Was taken in a cab, and left the station by a back entrance so that the public were utaware of the circum- stance. 'The medical officer in tharge at the. Infunnary has received a request from the politic not to allow the -woman to see any visitors. div.head: TIER IRISH LAND BILL.
div.p: TIER IRISH LAND BILL.

The debate,en the motion for tke second reading of the Irish Land Purchase Bill was resumed by Mr. PARNELL, who said he approved of the principle of the measure,, but believed that the bill was so designed under the circumstances of the present time as to render it impossible that that principle could be duly land efficiently carried out. The hon. gentleman stated at length his objections to the Government's proposals, land said the greatest danger of all was that the Govern- ment had not attempted to conciliate the national sentiment, but had treated the land question as though it were a purely agrarian question. He urged that before the bill left the House there should 'be drafted into it provisions dealing with the question of arrears, believing that if that were done this ativanse on the part ,of the Legislature would be appre- ciated and welcomed by the Irish people. Lord R&NDOLPH CIII7RCHILL replied to Mr. PARNELL, and remarked that it was just possible, from the expression which had fallen from the CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER and the SoLicrroa GENERAL for Ism-4.Np in.this debate, that the Government had it in their minds to make some proposals on the question of arrears. The noble Lord criticised some of the features of this kind of legislation, .but appealed to the House to let the hill go forward, and to turn its attention to the other business of the session. The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, referring to the charge that the Purchase Act did not benefit the congested districts, said those districts would be dealt with outside the lines of this Act by a proposal whieh would be a part of a larger plan on which he hoped the Government would be able soon to embark. The debate was continued by other hon. members, and at an advanced hour Sir William Hen- cormr took part in it. tilr. SMITH rose at midnight to move the closure, but a division on the main question was taken forthwith, with the following result :—For the second reading, 299.; against, 224; majority for, 75.

TERRIBLE EMPLOSION.—THREE LIVES Los.—A terrible explosion occurred on Wednesday morning on board a naphtha ship at Bristol, and resulted, it is feared, in the loss of three lives. The vessel was the United, of Jersey, which was laden with 310 barrels of naphtha, and intended leaving for London. About half-past eleven o'clock the whole neighbourhood of Bathurst Basin, where the vessel was lying, was alarmed by a violent explosion, and immediately the ship was enveloped in flames, which raged so furiously that for a considerable lime the adjoining shipping and warehouse property was in imminent danger. The crew of the vessel consisted of four persons, viz. Captain Cart- wright, the mate, an able seaman and a ,boy. These were all on board a few minutes seaman, the explosion, and the captain, mate and the boy have perished. The I able seaman was picked up in the harbour, and is now in the hospital suffering from a broken leg, the loss of a I foot, ancl other injuries. r CONFERENCE ON EDECAT/ON.—A conferencewas opened in Exeter Hall, on Tuesday, on the report of the Royal I Commission on Education. Mr. H. H. Fowler, M.P., who presided, stated the main objections to the report. which had rekindled animosities among the friends of education. Mr. Osborne Morgan, M.P., moved, Mr. Cosh= M.P., seconded, and Mr. T. Snape. (Liverpool) supported a resolution, which was carried, expressing the opinion that the recommendations made by the majority of the Royal Commission on some fundamental points were justly condemned by the minority as having been conceived in the interest of denominationalism rather than aiming at the establishment of a system of education on the broad basis of local support and popular management. Mr. Woodall, M.P., moved a resolution, which was passed unanimously, protesting against the suggested checks, in the report of the majority, on the supply of additional school accommodation, on ' the transfer of voluntary schools to School Boards, and other points. Another resolution advocated the extension of the School Board system. A meeting was held in Exeter Hall in the evening, under the presidency of Mr. Mun- della, when resolutions similar to those given above were adopted. Among the speakers on Wednesday were Mr. A. Acland, M.P., Sir U. Kay-Shuttleworth, M.P., Mr. C. Acland, M.P., the Rev. H. Price Hughes, Mr. P. W. Clayden, the Rev. Dr. Crosskey (Birmingham), the Rev. S. Barnett, the Rev. Guinness Rogers, the Rev. Brooke Lambert, and Mr. Carvell Williams. Resolution's con- demning the reactionary proposals of the majority of the Education Commission, but approving certain practical recommendations of the Commission, were unanimously agreed to, after which a preliminary com- mittee was appointed for the purpose of forming a National Education Committee. Dressmakers can buy no better sewing cotton than Bagley and Wright's, which for strenght Is uneceialled.—Advt.

div.p: NEW BOOKS, &c.

In the Great Writers series, published by Mr. Walter Scott, London, we have the" Lite of Heinrich Heine by William Sh.rp." A work of this kind is much needed for English readers many of whom are but newly acquainted with the subtle and many- sided genius of Heine. Alike in prose and in verse, be is unique amongst his feilows, and it is natural to want to know something more about him than cau be gleaned from his writings. This want Mr. Sharp satisfies. Himself a poet, he becomes a fitting biographer of a poet; and it is thus that Heine has something likejustiee done to him. This life will be new reading to many students, while to the general reader it will have all the freshness and interest of a novel. "Poems of Wild Life; selected and edited by Charles G. I). Roberts, MA." is the current issue of the Canter- bury Poets. Mr. Roberts furnishes an appropriate intro- duction in which he remarks, as to the milk-and-water literature which is current in the drawing-room, that "There has been so much talk of the repose of. conscious strength that one is apt to forget about the repose of conscious weakness." There is nothing of weakness, and little of repose, in these selections; they stir the pulse with a healthy glow • and give pictures of life in the far west and in Australia which cannot fail to interest those who study theta. A large number of authors are laid under contribution—from Cullen Bryant to Walt Whit- man—and the biographical notes as to each writer make the volume especially useful for reference purposes. In the Camelot series (published by the same firm) we have "The Teaching of Epictetus, being the Encheiridion of Epictetus, with selections from the Dissertations and Fragments." The work is translated from the Greek with an introduction and notes by Mr. T. W. Rolleston to whom the .ask has evidently been a labour of love. It was the aim of Epictetus "to stir the minds of his hearers towards the best things," and it has been the aim of the translator to ensure that the best things of Epictetus should be placed before the reader. The notes are extensive and painstaking; and there is besides an index of references of particular value. _ . .

" The Policeman's Lantern," also issued by Mr. Walter Scott, is a series of "Strange Stories of London Life," by Mr. James Greenwood, who is so well known as "The Amateur 'Casual." The lantern lights up some very dark corners, but society will be all the better for looking Into them. Mr. Greenwood handles delicate topics in a delicate style, and is as full of matter as an egg is full of meat. The stories are not mere padding; they are the outcome of careful inquiry and observation, and they bear upon them the impress of truth. We commend this shilling volume to those who, while desiring some- thing lively, like at the same time their readirqto be pro- fitable. Let " paterfam;" for instance, turn to the I chapter •en "Burglary made easy " ; he will, as the phrase is, ;find "something to his advantage." It comprises over 400 well-printed pages, and there are some scores of illustrations—some of them being artistic in the it-Wiest degree. There are besides over 30 maps and plans which have been specially prepared to render the work complete. As the preface remarks, the guide is "descriptive not only of the London and North-Western, and the Caledonian railways, but also of the associated services that connect with their mail and tourist expresses throughout England, Scotland, Wales and Ireland." div.head: HORRIBLE DEATH OF AN INFANT. AN INHUMAN MOTHER.
div.p: HORRIBLE DEATH OF AN INFANT. AN INHUMAN MOTHER.

An extraordinary case of a mother administering boil- ing hot food to her infant, was investigated on Saturday nicht, at the Foleshill Workhouse. by Dr. Iliffe, North Warwickshire coroner. The mather, whose name is Mary Page, entered the workhouse on the 18th of July last, beinc confined there three months subsequently. On the 2nd instant the workhouse nurse heard Page's elifld crying bitterly. and on entering the room observed the mother feeding it with boiling hot food. The nurse immediately took the child. Idling Page she was "munching" it. Pace replied, "If lam not ' munching' it, I will." The cbild's mouth was scalded, and death subsequently ensued. Dr. Orton said the lips and mucous membrane of the child's mouth were much scalded. The mouth became' uteerated, being a mass of sores, and the child died from exhaustion produced by the burns and want of fend. The jury returned a vet. diet to that effect, and passed an opinion that the mother gave the toed knowing that it was boilinr, and that some intention existed in her mind to injura trig *lid. The woman was subsequently arrested by the pude&

Warrington, P.G., Mr. Thomas' Roberts, P.C.S. ; Mr. William Croskill, D.D.G.M., Mr. Henry Kent, y.D.u.m., etc. The Secretary read letters of apology for non- attendance from Mr. Peter Leigh, Mr. Walter Milner, Mr. R. Mellor (Southport), and Mr. W. Houghton (secretary of the Crewe district), after which The CHAIRMAN explained that he stood in a position which should have been occupied by Alderman Har- rison, whose absence, caused no doubt by the severity of the weather, was regretted by all of them. (Hear, hear.) They had come together that evening for the purpose of honouring a good eld friend, Mr. Ray. He had never had the pleasure of meeting Mr. Ray before that evening, but when he saw such a number gathered together for the purpose of doing honour to any particu- lac man, he knew that that man must deserve great credit for some good which he had done. (Hear, hear.) When a lot of men, mostly engaged in working with their hands, were banding together and forming; an order, such'as his hearers were doing, be considered it was a credit to themselves, the town in which they lived, and the country at large. (Applause.) Every man who joined such a society must be an enemy to the work- house, for he believed Dia. if young men would join an order of that sort, and be careful in youth, they need never make the acquaintance of the bare walls of a workhouse for support in their old age. He believed that a man in any position of life ought to try not only to help himself, but his brother who was not quiet so well • off as himself. (Hear, hear.) When workingmen were found providing for the days of sick- ness, old age, and trouble, they ought to be assisted in every possible way. (Applause.) The usual loyal toasts having I.:wen given from the chair, the Secretary proposed "The Army, Navy, and Reserve Forces" which was responded to by Captain Ridgway.—The Vice-chairman gave "The Town and Trade of Warrington" and the Chairman responded. Captain RIDGWAY said he had been entrusted with the pleasant duty of making the presentation to their retir- ing secretary, Mr. W. E. Ray. He had held the office of , arbitrator for three years, and he never yet had been called upon to settle any difficulty. That showed not I only how well the rules of the lodge had been formed, but how efficiently the officers had done their duty. (Applause.) He could not let the opportunity pass , without thanking Mr. Ray for the valuable assistance he had rendered at Sankey in connection with the Sunday school. He had worked equally well for the lodge— (applause)—during the ten years in which he had held the post of secretary, and on behalf of the members of the Mermaid Lodge he had very great pleasure in pre- senting that beautiful timepiece to Mr. Ray, and with it an emblem of the order. (Applause.) He trusted that whenever Mr. Ray looked at that clock he would remember that the occasion on which it had been pre- sented to him was one of the happiest and pleasantest levenings he had ever spent—long might he be spared to see that clock ornament his dining-room. (Applause.) Mr. RAY, who was cordially received, thanked the members of the lodge for the great kindness they bad exhibited by presenting him with that handsome testi- monial, and Captain Ridgway for the kind manner in which he had spoken of him. (Hear, hear.) Referring to the early history of that lodge, he said it was started in 1811 as a dividing society, and the members were in the habit of spending more money on the, inner man than in providing for the sick and needy. (Laughter.) Coming down to later days, the lodge 10 years age numbered 160 members, and had £l9O to its credit; at the present time it numbered 196 members, and had to, its credit £372. (Applause.) . There had been spent during that time, in sick, funeral, and medical benefits. £2,151. (Hear, hear.) Speaking of the funds, he said' he would like the Town Council to give friendly societies an opportunity of investing more money at 3 per cent with them, instead of being compelled to leave it in the bank and receive only 2,1 per cent, for it. (Hear, hear.). Mr. J. Ray then proposed "The Order of Druids and the Warrington District."—Mr. Tnoxas RODERTS in responding, said the diStrict was formed some 52'or 5.5 years ago, and had always been on the increase, both financially and numerically. It comprised 12 lodges. with a membership of 1,200 members, and a worth of £3,742 2s. '6d.; the funeral fund, was £1,039 17s. 7d.; widow and orphan's fund. £756 ss. 64d.; and family funeral fund, £1,649 16s. 2d.; making the total worth of the Warrington and District Society of Druids, £7,188 is. 10d.—Other toasts of a complimentary nature fol- lowed.—During the evening pengs were given by Messrs. Wm. Massey, James Ray, sea., Henry Sant,, James Ray, jun., Walter Ray, Inn., and others.

div.head: SCHIEVER QUARTET AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE SCHIEVER QUARTET AT WARRINGTON.

On Monday evening a second concert, by the mem- bers of the Schiever Quartet Party, was given in the Co-operative Hall, before an audience which, though small in point of numbers, included many of the elite of the town and neighbourhood. A commend- able effort is .being made to secure, for lovers of classical chamber music, a series of three concerts of this character during the current season, and, though we can hardly imagine that the measure of support accorded to Monday's conceit-will, be con+ sidered, by the promoters, to be altogether satisfac- tory, it is to be hoped that they will be sufficiently' encouraged to carry out the scheme in its entirety.. Of the concert itself, we can speak only in terms of the highest praise. The quartet, as on the previous occasion. comprised.—Herr Ernest Schiever as Ist violin; Mr. Thomas Shaw, 2nd violin; Herr Carl Courvoisier, viola ; and Herr Carl Fuchs, violoncellos Miss Frederika E. Taylor occupying her accustomed place as soprano vocalist. The programme included two complete quartets for the strings by Beethoven and Mendelssohn, and a third made up of two excerpts from the works of Schubert and Cherubini. Although there were, of course, in the first two, many striking and I.eautiful passages of melody and harmony on which the the ear could dwell, the two contrasted movements by Schubert and Cherubini were certainly not inferior in interest. Indeed, judged by the manifestations of a discriminating audience, they must be acknowledged to have formed the piece de resietance of the evening. Herr Schiever's violin solo, " Gondoliera " and " Moto perpetuo " (Fr. Ries), gave further proof, were such needed, of the perfection to which he has brought his knowledge of the teehnique of his instrument. Tke sewn*: movement is, ef course, a very trying one for the instrumentalist, taxing, as it does, the executive powers to the utmost. As a feat of memory alone, it was, in no small degree, a wonder- ful performance, Herr Fuchs appeared also in the cltwoctlr of eolorsti Ana 1-4.layed the " Traumprci" of al Schumann, li and the "azurics pf Popper, in n style that the audience would take z;.• W:014 or their demand for an additional item.. ihth hi tone and style Herr Fuchs' playing is alike 'admirable. Miss Taylor sang an air from Sir M. Costa's "Eli," and the old Irish melody "Rich and Rare„' sweetly, and with taste, the most charming characteristics of her singing being a clear enunciation and an unaffected simplicity of manner. Mr. Bird played the accompaniments to the songs and the .instru- mental solos with skill and excellent taste.

"37, Gonsalva Road, Wandsworth Road, London, S.W., July 19th, 1888.—DEAR SIR.-It is with great pleasure I offer you this unsolicited testimonial. My husband was for some time losing flesh, and getting generally weak, until at last he could no longer follow his employment, and was obliged to give up. For 23 weeks he was laid up, and was quite unable to work at all, being attended during part of that time by a London physician. On advice I had him removed to our home in Devonshire. Two doctors there said, after examining him, that he would never do any more work. Seeing Your Moonseed Bitters advertised in the Wee/ay Record (Dorset), I determined to try a bottle. The first bottle gave him relief from the pain at his heart, which all the doctors' medicine could not do. He has now taken ten bottles of Moonseed Bitters, and is as strong and well as ever he was in his life. I have no hesitation in saying that Moon- seed Bitters has saved his life. He, in recompense to you, can only offer a personal interview to anyone who this letter may interest.—Believe ins, Sir, yours very truly, HILDA GRAY. . '' ..
