THE EXAMINER,
- - -- - SATURDAY. NOVEMBER 24. 1888.

The Government are guilty of an unprecedented :and discreditable thing in bringing forward, and -trying to force through,at an adjourned Sessions, : 's a measure such as the new Irish Land Bill. It involves five millions of the money of the British taxpayer, and they deal with it as lightly as if it were a matter of five pounds. It was understood fact it was an engagement—when a late Sessions was arranged,that no new business should be brought forward about which there would be ay likelihood of contention. It was irregular on the face of it to think of anything else, seeing that an adjournment was prcposed, and important measures were being sacrificed, in order to make . • sure of supply, and of carrying bills through which had already been more or less discussed. Of course, if something new had suddenly arisen, it would be the duty of the Government to ask Parliament to deal with the matter; but there is no sugges- tion of anything of the kind. The Land Act it is Proposed to extend, in this summary fashion, has been in operation for some time; and if it were Bought to obtain "something on account," to con- tinue operations until Parliament resumes work next year, the proposal might have been mentioned 'before the adjournment, just as well as after it. Indeed, Mr. GLADSTONE, as leader of the Opposi- tion, has shown himself not unwilling, even at the eleventh hour,to accommodate the Ministry in this respect. But they desire something more than this; they desire at the fag-end of a fagging Se,ssion to commit the House and the nation to a Policy from which it might afterwards be difficult to retire; while going forward is likely to prove disastrous in the highest degree. Mr. GLADSTONE'S Irish Land Bill was denounced as something monstrous because it proposed to deal with the 'question of land purchase on a largo scale. But

so far as the money goes, it will come to the same I thing if we are to go on providing five millions after five millions in this hasty and slip-shod fashion. There is, however, a vast difference between Mr. GLADSTONE'S SCh9 me and the proposal of the Government. In the one case ample provision I was made for protecting the taxpayers. Security was taken, and that secruity, we have always believed,was of a substantial kind. In the present case , there is practically no security; the State becomes the direct creditor of the Irish tenant—a principle which might work tolerably well amongst better-class farmers, but one which is calculated te prove utterly mischievous if it be carried through from top to bottom. Five millions have been granted; other five millions are to follow immediately, if the Government are to have their way, and no one can say how many millions more. But this much, at least, is certain,that the extension of the grants means that the less prosperous will gradually come forward as applicants. Some of them will succeed; some of them will fail, and then—what? The State, to secure itself, will be compelled to resort to eviction. It is bud enough for the British people to look on and see the Irish landlords evict Irish tenants for arrears ; but it will be a hundred times worse to look on and see the same things done on behalf of the State. Mr. GLADSTONE'S bill avoided all this by making the Irish Executive responsible, and by keeping safirient money in hand from customs and excise for the payment of interest. The security he provided was derided by people who never took the trouble to study his measure; but what will the Dissentients in the country have to say now when there is no security at all? It is a significant thing that there have been, according to the statement of the SOLICITOR- GENERAL for Ireland, 7,711 applications in Ulster for land purchase under Lord ASHBOLTRNE'S Act. The total of the other three provinces combined is only 6,627. Granted that this points to the prosperous and thrifty condition of Ulster, as com- pared with the other provinces, it points also to the fact that the poorer class of tenants—these who are really in most need of help—are not being benefited. We may grant another five millions under Lord ASHBOURNE'S Act, or we may grant fifty; but it will not settle the land question in Ireland. It will meet the wishes of the tenants who are not in the clutches of their landlords, and it will delight the landlords by putting money in their purses. The Government mean, of course, to please them, however it may fare with the rest of the community; but it is for the taxpayer to say whether he will be bled in this random and ill- considered fashion. Let it be understood that we do not begrudge the five millions,if it can be proved that it will be a permanent benefit to the mass , of the Irish peasantry. But there is no attempt to prove anything of the kind. It will do nothing of the kind; it will be no relief, as Mr. GLAD- STONE showed in his powerful speech on Monday evening, to those who are sutler- ing eviction through being over-burdened with arrears which they cannot pay. These arrears are the Damocles' sword hanging over the head of the Irish tenant. The hair by which it is suspended is too often, alas! cut by the Irish landlord, who thus disables his victim, if he does not absolutely deprive him of life. The right way to move is to grant just sufficient money to keep the act going—not to tie ourselves for several years by a grant of five millions "at one fell swoop." This done, as Mr. GLADSTONE'S amendment puts it, it becomes "expedient, espe- cially in view of the lamentable sufferings caused by recent evictions in Ireland, to extend the pro- visions of the Land Law (Ireland) Act, 1887, so as to empower the Land Court to reduce or cancel the arrears of rents found to be excessive, as well as to deal with the rents themselves, after example of the legislation recently and beneficially applied to the crofters' holdings in Scotland." In other words, having dealt reasonably and justly by the crofters of Scotland, we ought to proceed to deal reasonably and justly with the peasantry of I Ireland.

"SOME economic and moral aspects of luxury" was the title of an interesting paper which Pro- fessor J. MAcCurrN read, on Tuesday evening, before the members of the Warrington Literary and Philosophical Society. Two or three points were touched on which, as it seems to us, the well-to- do would do well to consider. The first is as to giving preference to "such luxuries as are durable to those that are perishable." Money is more rapidly made in this generation than kiver before in the history of mankind; but the mass of the people do not get their full share of the good things of life because, along with large incomes, there is large expenditure on things that are of no permanent value—in other words, on perishable luxury. Dinners, for instance, have become banquets. There is sometimes as much spent in a single public entertainment of this kind as would keep a hundred poor people for a year. A local mayor's dinner to forty or fifty people makes ducks and drakes of a hundred pounds; and who, next day, can be said to be any the better for it? Of flowers, which are also perish- able, humanity sees altogether too little; but happily they are not necessarily costly. Their beauty is not in proportion to their rarity; but rarity is sought by the rich ; and luxury in this respect becomes extravagance when, to take a common case, absurdly fancy prices are paid for fancy orchids. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN is reputed to have a weakness in this direction. It stands against him with the masses; it has long been regarded as showing an aristocratic, rather than a demo- erotic taste. The flower reveals the man. There is selfishness in luxury of this kind; and this violates what Professor MACCUNK calls the second canon of choice, namely, the preference for unselfish to selfish luxury. Some men there are who spend fabulous sums in laying out parks and gardens, and, by way of completion of their plans, they put up a high wall,so that nonebut a privileged few may enjoy the beauty which has been brought into being. This is selfish luxury—selfish to the point of brutality. It is the charm of Southport--to its credit be it said .--that the reverse of this holds good. Every house has its garden; and every garden is, as it should be, a benefaction to the public. Books are a luxury; they are the luxury of luxuries to a well ordered mind. Wetake from the rates, and erect buildings, and fill them, in order that all who desire to do so may constantly delight in them. Libraries are not classed as perishable luxuries; nor are they selfish luxuries except in such cases as that of the Warrington Library, where the law is violated to keep the Library "select." It is a suggestive commentary upon the selfish luxury of the classes that books which have been bought with the money of the ratepayers cannot be lent to tho ratepayers except upon subscription, or a fee—both of which are illegal. Whilst touching this subject, we may mention that the trustees of the defunct Workmen's Club expect to have a balance of some £6OO or £7OO. How would it be to apply it towards freeing the Library ? It would certainly best meet the needs and wishes of the working-men in the town, by whom, and on whose behalf, the money was

Smokers havCi-a,nother consolation. It has been proved by recent experiment that "tobacco smoke retards the development of some kinds of bacteria, while it entirely prevents the development of others." It comes to this, that nicotine is poisonous to bacteria as well as to men. The weed is consoling, but in a deadly sort of way.

The Government have been guilty of a bit of practice which is smart, rather than creditable, in getting the Land Purchase Bill printed before :leave was given for its introduction. It is, it is stated, entirely' without precedent ; but there is no one so unconstitutional as your Constitutional- ist—especially when he has a " job " in hand.

According to a London contemporary, the Scotch members have received private intimation from the Chancellor of the Exchequer that if they will support the Wheel and Van Tax Bill the Act shall not apply to Scotland. But is not this a species of bribery and corruption? And if the Act is not good enough for Scotland, why should it be good enough for England?

Considerable stir has been made by the protest in the "Nineteenth Century" against the system of examination; but there is no likelihood of the examination system being abolished. It has its faults, but it has great merits. What is wanted is that it shall be so directed as to find the best quali- ties of a candidate, or of a pupil. We cannot go back; examination of some kind there must be.

Hero is an item of news of a new kind:— "Simon Ready, of Heywood, Lancashire, a mem- ber of the National League, was shot on Monday night on the highway near that place. The bullet pierced his leg. The police made one arrest." This looks like turning the tables on the Leaguers; it is quite a break in the monotony of the ordinary way of doing things.

Nearly half a century has elapsed since Maggie Fox, of New York State, became famous as a "medium." She has now confessed that the "spirit rapping" was accomplished by a peculiar faculty she has of manipulating her toes! There is weeping and wailing, and gnashing of teeth amongst the spiritualists ; but Maggie cloesrii; re; she can snap her fingers—and her toes—at them.

A Vienna correspondent says he hears on good authority that Herr Radowitz, the German Ambas- sador to the Porte, was promised the co-operation of Turkey in the suppression of slavery on tho coast of the Red Sea. Turkey promised England the same thing; she will, when it suits her, promise anything to anybody. It is not the promise—it is the performance which is generally at fault, for that is too much in the nature of a farce.

Mr. Jolley was in a great hurry at the meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians, on Wednesday, to suggest that the females of the Workhouse should have half a pint of beer to their Christmas Dinner. Mr. Jolley does not seem to profit by experience. There was a limit to the supply of liquor last year ; but for all that some of the inmates got "jolly well drunk." Guardians will do well to refresh their memories before refreshing the inmates.

"Truth" says :—" Probably Lady Mountmorres was not aware why her husband was shot, and it would have been cruel to allude to the circum- stances when she was a witness before the Com- mission. But, if what I hear be true, the per- petrator of the deed is well-known, and the deed was done to avenge a private wrong. The Fenians, the secret societies, the evicted tenants, and the National League, had no more to do with the matter than I had."

The Warrington Branch of the English Church Union is alive, and it is disposed to strike back— judging from the meeting held on Monday even- ing. Mr. C. S. Burgess took exception to the following statement put in circulation in the town :—" The Eastward position is a direct step towards Popery." There is no denying, however, that it is in the direction of the Pope. His Holi- ness resides in Rome. That is "Eastward" is it not?

With regard to the suggestion that lectures should be given, Mr. John White humorously remarked that they would have greater difficulty about getting audiences than lecturers. It does look had when there is a "beggarly array of empty benches." But there is such a thing as getting used to that. Almost any day in the week,in some of our great Cathedrals, the officials outnumber the congregation. The officials are, of course, paid to put in an appearance, and that does make a difference.

In another portion of the paper, we give the last of the present series of articles on Ireland by "Home Rule." Written as they have been throughout in a temperate and argumentative style, they have, we have every reason to believe, been highly appreciated by those who are honestly seeking light on the great question of the day. We thank our correspondent for his valuable contributions; and, as gratitude is said to be a sense of favours to come, we venture to express the hope that we shall hear from him again.

Answering a question put to him in the House of Commons, on Tuesday, Mr. Stanhope said he was aware that an English firm, which had received a contract for sword bayonets, had discharged some English and engaged German hands in their place. The reason was that the industry had almost died out of this country, and Germans must necessarily be brought over to do the work. They would, however, return home soon. We do not blame the Ministry for "encouraging foreign labour" under the circumstances, but if a Liberal Government had done a similar thing what a row there would have been! The Fair Traders would have shouted themselves black in the face.

Mr. Justice Wills,judging from his charge to the grand jury at Carlisle, on Monday, seems to think the Criminal Law Amendment Act is working badly. "It should not, he said, housed simply as a means of assault upon the ordinary immoralities of country life, because that was not the way they could subdue them. They must attack them through the heart and the conduct of life. Thecrim- inal law should, in his judgment, be reserved for something that was pretty serious." The fact is I the Act has failed in its object; it was intended to reach rich rascals; but it does not in its actual operation go much beyond what his lordship aptly describes as " the ordinary immoralities of country life." The big fish avoid the net; it is the little fish thatare caught.

Lord Randolph Churchill supports the Five Millions Bill, but he evidently thinks it has had features. On Thursday night he said—" The security offered for the advances was totally insifflicient—(laughter)—but the risk arising from an insufficient security when applied to filr6 , millions might not he great. He entirely agreed with those who said it would never do to make the State the immediate landlord of the Irish tenants." Again—" He supported the Bill because it was not a large Bill. (Laughter.) It was rather like the poor woman who looked upon her illegitimate child and said, 'Please, ma'am, it is only a little one.'" (Laughter.) Lord Randolph regards the measure as a bad one, but he backs it because "it might have been worse."

AiABILING FISH AT Isiosamw fire took place at Rllies music repository, situate in the centre of Northwich, on Monday night, which endangered the whole town, the surrounding build- ings being constructed mainly of wood. The family had gone to a concert, and the children had to be rescued through the windows by the neighbours. The stock was destroyed and the building gutted, but the energetic action of the brigade prevented a general conflagration. The loss is great and only partially covered by insurance. RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AitITHORITY. The fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Thursday. Colonel Ashton presided, and there were also present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Mclntyre:. Aaron, Weir, Brindreth, Stokes, Heywood, W. Whitlow, Lewis; H. Linaker (clerk): W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk), and J. Farrington (inspector of nuisances). BYE-LAWS FOR APPLETON.-A letter was read from the overseers of Appleton approving. of-a copy of bye-laws that had been submitted to, them.—On the- motion of Mr. Weir the bye-laws were adopted. OVERSEERS TO BE PROSECLITEDt-it was reported that the overseers of FrcAlsham had failed to pay calls-made upon them with regard to a special rate.—Mr. Aaron said that if all the overseers in the Union did thesame as the' overseers of Frodsham where would the money come I from to carry on the woe:. of the Sanitary Authority? He thought that they should have no quarter shown at alland , he moved that the Frodsham overseers be summoned at once before the magistrates at Runcorn Petty Sessions.' —Mr. Weir seconded the proposal, which was agreed to. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT—The Medical Officer (Dr. Adams) reported the occurrence of starlet fever within the district. Three cases (a mother and two children) had occurred at a hut belonging to the Manchester Ship Canal Company, at Acton Grange. With most com- mendable promptitude, the authorities of the Manches- ter Ship Canal contract at once sanctioned his proposal to negotiate for the transfer of these three cases to the Warrington Fever Hospital. In connection with the above, and in view of the necessity of transferring other cases of infectious disease to the care of an adjoining sanitary district, it was a matter for consideration if the time had not come, especially in consequence of the recent passing of the new Local Government Act, for that authority now at length to entertain his previous recommendation (embodied in successive annual reports) of supplying a most urgent want by erecting a small hospital for infectious diseases at some convenient locality within its own boundaries. He had further to , report that three cases of scarlet fever of a mild charac- ter had occurred within the township of Halton. He understood that a few cases of a mild character had also occurred at Weston Point.—A short discussion took place with regard to the medical officer's recommendation to erect a small hospital, and Mr. Mclntyre moved that the Clerk be instructed to write to the Warrington Corpora- tion in order to ascertain on what conditions they would be prepared to take cases in their hospitals. 1 This was all the business of public interest.

SELF Murttsvon.—Mr. Cunnah, the workhouse master, reported that a person. named James Milling- ton, of Runcorn, 37 years of age, had mutilated him- self by severely cutting two fingers of his left hand ard I the little toe of his right foot with a knife. He lad been admitted to the casual ward, and wanted to go to stone breaking, but on being given oakum to pick he said he was too ill to work. The medical officer, how- ever, said that nothing ailed the man but indigestion. It was after being submitted to the medh al officer that he committed the mutilation.—Mr. Taylor thought it was the hard stones that had given the man indigestion. —Mr. Brandreth suggested that he be prosecuted.—Mr. Speakman thought it was more a case for the asylum than the sessions.—The Deputy-Clerk said the medical officer of the house said the man was perfectly sane.— Mr. Stokes : Would there be good food at the asylum P A-Member : Yes, of course.—Mr. Aaron said the food that was given in that workhouse, together with no work, would bring on indigestion. (Laughter.) —Mr. Mclntyre said an hour's resolute chastisement with a birch rod was what was required —Mr. Aaron said he knew more about the man than all the rest of the Board nut together, and he moved that he be prosecuted. —Mr. Brandreth seconded this proposal, which was agreed to. Cnnisvmss Dumen.—lt was resolved that the usual Christmas dinner be given to the inmates. The rest of the business was formal.

DRUNKEN WIVES AND HARDWORING HUSBANDS AT WIDNES. EXTRAORDINARY WOUNDING CASE. On Thursday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, Henry Murphy, a chemical labourer. of 23, Marsh-street, was charged with having caused grievous bodily harm to Bridget Murphy, his wife. It appeared from the evidence that Mrs. Murphy got drunk on Monday afternoon and when the prisoner arrived home at a quarter to six his tea was not prepared. According to Mrs. Winifrid Sweeney. who.with her husband, occupies the two rooms of the house, a quarrel ensued. She heard loud sealing and noise, for about a quarter of an hour, and then the prisoner left the house. Shortly afterwards Mrs.. -Sweeney went into the next room, and found Mrs. Murphy lying on the sofa. Blood was issuing from beneath her Clothes' and she was also bleed- ing about the nose. . Mrs. Margaret Fay bore similar testimony, and it was stated that the Prisoner had not alleged that his wife was unwell. At eleven o'clock the same night Dr. Hutchinson visi ad the house, and found the. woman almost bled to death. She was in a state of collapse. Each side of her face was bruised and blackened, and there was a clot of blood in one of her nostrils. There was considerable heemorrage from the womb. This bleeding was not a natural process; violence must have been used. A fall against the table might have caused it, but it was not probable. Mrs. Murphy, who was seriously cautioned, was sworn, and stated that she was stupidly drunk when her husband came home. Her husband did not touch her. She attempted to get his tea ready, and fell against the table, which was overturned, and the crockery broken. Her face came in contact with the wall. Afterwards she felt a queer sensation coming oacr her, and she lay down on the soft. Her husband went out and Mrs. Sweeny came in. She sent for Dr. Hutchinson; at 7 o'clock, but he was not in. PC. Dean deposed that when apprehended the prisoner said "I never touched her."—The Magistrates considered it was a case for a jury to decide, and committed the prisoner to Quarter Sessions for triat Mrs. Murphy applied that he should be admitted to bail,, so that he could work for the children. He was innocent of the charge. He was a sober man, and she took drink.—The Bench decided to liberate the prisoner, on hail, himself in £4O; and two sureties of £2O each.—At Widnes Police Court, on Wed- nesday, before Mr. H. Wade-Deacon, a labourer named Wm. Sant., of 44 Vintoria-st., was charged with haying caused grievous bodily harm to his wife,, Sarah A. Sant. It appeafeil from the evidence that on Tuesday at noon, ' when the prisoner got home for his dinner, he found his wife drunk. She was in the same condition in the evening, when he had finished his work, and there was no tea prepared. A quarrel took place, and the prisoner knocked his wife down, and kicked her with his clog, causing an ugly and dangerous wound on the woman's head.—Dr. (AKA-0 certified that the woman was unable to appear, and the prisoner was remanded for a week.

WIDNES. The past week has been noted for the prevalence of high winds, frequently accompanied by heavy rain. The weather was at its worst on Tuesday. A fierce gale swept across both towns during the whole of the day, and at noon there was a brief, but violent, thunderstorm. The lightning flashes were exceptionally vivid, and the thunder peals loud and prolonged, while rain descended in torrents. On Runcorn Bridge the violence of the storm was felt in its full force, and to those com- pelled to cross, the task was not only very unpleasant, but difficult. Traffic on the river was almost suspended. Several flats, notably tho,e of Messrs. Evans and Co., the colliery proprietors, were turned out with re-inforced crews, because of the urgent necessity of delivering the cargoes, and they experienced great hardship in reaching their destination. The Duke's Packets also succeeded in carrying on a portion of the trade of the port of Runcorn. The Village Belle, of Dublin, was success- fully docked, and the captain reported that he had lostone of his hands off the Great Ormes Head. The barque Thomas Bowstead, of Barrow, laden with bone ash, from Rio Grande to Weston Point, went ashore on the rocks at the mouth of the Weaver. The vessel was in tow of one of the Weston Point steam tugs when the hawser parted, and the vessel drifted as stated. Fortunately she has sustained little damage. No fatalities have been reported.

div.head: MR. BRUNNER ON THE LAND PURCHASE.
div.p: MR. BRUNNER ON THE LAND PURCHASE.
BILL.

On Saturday evening Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P. for the Northwich Division, was one of the prin- cipal speakers at a Liberal meeting at Knutsford, and proposed the following resolution:—" That this meeting condemns the action of the present Government is its cruel administration of an unjust Coercion Act, and hereby expresses its unabated confidence in the Liberal leaders, believing that their policy of conciliation and justice to Ireland is the best calculated to promote and to maintain the integrity of the empire." Re said they would remember very well, how two years ago their oppo- nents, the Conservatives and those who called themselves Liberal Unionists, told them that the people of these four kingdoms had a full right to the benefut of just and equal laws; and an equality of treatment as between Great Britain and Ireland was die one point upon which they laid the greatest stress. How far had those fair-seeming promises been kept? (Hear, hear.) Those pledges had been thrown to the idle winds,they had enacted a Coercion Act, more bitter, more mean, and more cruel than any which had ever been passed by any Parliament. ("Shame.") But their hopes of what they would consider good results from the passing of that Act had been entirely frustrated. (Applause.) He oonld tell that audience, that from what he knew of the Irish members they were in no way dismayed by tifat terrible Coercion Act. (Cheers.) He could; from personal knowledge, tell them that the people in Ireland had just as stout hearts, nay, stotVer hearts, as ever. (Loud cheers.) Referring to the fact that next week Mr. Balfour was to move the extension of what was called Lord Ashburne's Act, M. Brunner asked if Mr. Gladstone was not in the right when he insisted that there should be some- body responsible in Ireland for the collection of rents? Mr. Gladstone proposed, as they knew very well, two years ago, that the credit of the State should be pledged in the first instance to the amount of fifty millions, and the ratepayers were to be absolutely secured. (Hear, hear.) There was no rent to be paid by those small farmers in Ireland directly to the ratepayers. The whole of the revenue of Ireland—the license taxes, the custom house, the excise, the income tax, and every possible tax—was to be gathered together, and, as Mr. Gladstone phrased it, was to pass through the neck of a bottle, and at the mouth of a bottle was to be placed an officer, paid by the ratepayers and responsible to the ratepayers, who was to receive the whole of the taxes, and out of the gross revenue of Ireland was to stop what was due to the ratepayers before one penny was to be paid towards the purchase of the property. (Applause.) Mr. Gladstone next week meant to meet Mr. Balfour' proposal for the extension of Lord Ashbourne's Act which had had the effect of putting them in direct rela- tion with the small farmers of Ireland, by the following amendment :—" That in lieu of proceeding again to vote the sum of five millions so as to place the State in the direct relation of landlord to the Irish occupier under the Provisions of the Purchase of Land (Ireland) Act, 1885, it is expedient, especially in view of the lamentable sufferings caused by recent evictions in Ireland, to extend the provisions of the Land Law (Ireland) Act, 1281, so as to empower the Land Court to reduce orl cancel the arrears of rent found to be excessive, as wel as to deal with the rents themselves after the example of the leg,is'ation recently and benefically applied i to the crofters' holdings n Scotland." Believing, firstly, that he might trust Mr. Gladstone on a matter of finance—(hear. hear)—and secondly, that he might trust him always to deal justly between man and man, he was going into the fight, which began on Monday, in the highest spirits. (Cheers.) Alluding to the last portion of the resolution, Mr. Brunner said he remembered having seen, and seen it -with a thrill of pride, in Liverpool, when her Majesty the Queen honoured that city by a visit, a very long list, put up on banners,of the names of sovereignsof England for 1,000 years, and not 150 years. This empire was a thousand years old, and during that time there had been a great many Parliaments. The empire existed in the last century ; the empire existed and was strong when there was a Parliament in Dublin—(cheers)—the empire had grown and flourished whilst they added Parliament after Parliament. We had to-day no fewer than 24 Parliaments in the British Empire, and we were all the better, all the stronger, for it, and if that 24 were made into 25 it would not destroy the integrity of the empire. (Loud cheers.) There were a good many ways of destroying the integrity of the empire, and it seemed to him that the Tory Government, headed by Lord Salisbury, was taking one of them. (Hear, hear.) It had seemed to those who sat in the House of Commons that they were within an ace of losing a large slice of the British Empire—he meant the Dominion of Canada. About a year ago the Govern- ment sent over to the United States a gentleman whose tongue sometimes ran away with his better judgment, he meant "my lord Chamberlain." (Laughter.) That emissary of theirs. despatched on a mission of peace, deemed it right to utter words that seemed calculated to set our countrymen across the herring-pond by the ears. That injudicious action on the part of the Tory Government had recently been followed by an absolutely incomprehensible and ludicrous blunder by our repre- sentative at Washington. They knew that the British Minister at Washington was only a fortnight ago desired to take himself out of the country because his presence in the United States was no longer:acceptable to the American Government. He believed there was a great deal too much common sense on both sides of the matter for us to quarrel so despera-ely as to go to war, t+ut when this country sent over to America a man trained in diplomacy who was yet • green enough to be taken in by a sharp American news- paper reporter, well, if he got a slap in the face, it seemed to him that he deserved it. (Hear, hear.) Now, her Majesty's Government, responsible for the integrity of the empire, had the incredible folly to offer to send to Queensland, which was crammed with Irish- men, a resident magistrate as governor. (Ironical laughter, and hisses.) Mr. Brunner concluded with a criticism of Mr. Balfour, and resumed his seat amid loud applause. The resolution was supported by Mr, Piers. Maliony, M.P., and carried.

QUININE BITTERS MANUFACIVRING CO., (LIMITED).— The statutary meeting of this Company was held at the Office of the company's solicitors, 8, Old Quay, on Thurs- day. The chairman,Mr. Geo. H. Barclay,remarked that there were no accounts or report to present to the met- ing e but he had pleasure in stating that since the busi- ness had been taken over by the company it had con- tinued in a most flourishing condition, and had already earned sufficient to pay 10 per cent on the paid up capital to March 31, 1880. The directors have resolved that an interim dividend at the rate of ten per cent per annum be paid up to Nov. 30, 1888, to be paid as soon after that date as possible. THE PARNELL INQUIRIL—On Tuesday the Parnell Com- mission resumed its sittings. Several witnesses were examined. Lizzie Curtin detailed the circumstances of the murder of her father in November, 1885. At the funeral she was hooted and laughed at by the people; her pew in the chapel was taken away, and her family were boycotted until compelled to leave the neighbour- hood. on Wednesday, Mr. Reid, Q.C., referring to the comments in the "Kerry Sentinel" as to the proceed- ings of the Commission, intimated that he had com- municated his views to Mr. E. Harrington, and that, as Mr. Harrington had not thought fit to adopt them, he was not in a position to say anything further. Ques- tioned by the President, Mr. Harrington said that he accepted responsibility for what appeared in his paper. After consultation with his colleagues the President imposed a fine of £5OO. The cross-examination of Miss Curtin was proceeded with, and amongst the other witnesses called was Nora Fitzmaurice, who spoke of the circumstances under which her father was murdered at Lixnaw. Mr. Maurice Lennard, agent for Lord Ken- mare, was under examination when the Court ad- journed. On Thursday, Mr. Leonard, agent to Lerd Kenmare, said that prior to 1880 there were very few evictions on Lord Kenmare's estate. The Flan of Cam- ' paign had been adopted on the estate. The National League was now as strong as ever. In cross-examin- ation the witness said that General Buller had intervened more than once to put dawn evictions. He put pres- sure on the landlords. Witness was averse to evictions. He would not evict very poor tenants.—lnspector Hug- gins (recalled) deposed to a series of outrages in 1880-81 at Castleisland, where a branch of the Land League was established, with a man named Timothy Horan as secretary. MANCHESTER RANGRUS TEAMS).—A. match between the above teams was played. on the Lower House-lane ground on Saturday,afternoon. In the former part of the game the home team had the best of it, but scored nothing higher than minors, of which they obtained eleven to the Rangers none. On the change of ends, Widnes continued to press, sad added a few more minors, while Manchester succeeded In getting one. Two tries were at length gained -for Widnes by Holt and Minton, after Bingham had managed to register one, but in the three instances the plats kick was a failure. The*enal score stood, Widnes. one goal, three tries, and 15 minors; Manchester Rangers, one minor._

...... ST. HELENS RECS "A " v. RuiticoßN RECS IsT. Played at Boundary-road. St. Helens, before about 1,560 spectators. The following were the teams. Recreation. —Greenall, full back; H. Gerrard, W. Matthews, and G. Bolton, three-quarters; J. Turton and J. Peachey, half-backs ; Holt (captain), Grainger, Adamson, Richard- son, Dean, Mather, Matthews, Tatlock, and Pendlebury, forwards. Runcorn.—Wishead, full back; Burton, Houghton, and Robinson, three-quarters; Jones and Cauley. half-backs; Lowe (captain), J. Acton, F. Acton, Gittens, Davies, Stubbs, Sutherton, Jonas, and Kirslev, forwards. Holt, the home team's captain, kicked Off against the wind, and Robinson returned well into the Recreation's half. The backs on both sides exhibited some good kicking, neither side gaining any advantage until Matthews got over the line,but Grainger, who tried the place, failed. After a very fast game, in which the home team had some bad luck, the final score was: St. Helens Recreation "A" one try and six minors, Runcorn Recreation Ist two minors. WIDNES v. MANCHESTER RANGERS.—The above teams , faced each other on the ground of the latter at Rusholme, before nearly 2,000 spectators. A fine game was wit- nessed. Widnes seemed to have the best of the game throughout; but lost in the scoring, lathe former part of the play each side obtained a goal from a free kick, Plumpton landing the first and A. Hamnett the secOnd. Three minors were afterwards added to the visitors' smite, And when half time was called the score stood at one goal and three Minors for Widnes, and one goal for the Rangers. Immediately after the change, Kiddie for the visitors took the oval over the home territory, and secured a try near the touch line, which Plumpton failed at converting into the major point. Widnes afterwards added four minors in quick succession. The home men had now almost given up all hopes of gaining another point, when the tables suddenly turned, and a different aspect was lent to the game by Hamnett rushing over the line and registering a try near the posts, which he successfully turned into a goal. Play had only resumed a few minutes when time was called, the score being— Rangers 2 goals, to Widnes 1 goal, 1 try, and 7 minors. Teams :—Widnes : Bingham, back; Plumpton, Parkinson, Hartles, and Clarke, three-quarter backs; Farrell and Howard, half backs ; Kiddie, Smith, Hardman, Hughes Pennington. Barber, Gandy, and Williams, forwards. Rangers :J. Gadd. back; H. Radcliffe, A. Hamnett, and C. G. Parkinson, three-quarter backs; S. Taylor, and P. Mceham, half backs; Herbert Hasleham, G. Pollard, A. M'Dougal, E. Mee, R Hamnett, H. Hamnett, W. Storer, W. G. Scorer, and T. Common, forwards. Itencoma V. °Lori/kn.—Saturday was the worst day experienced by footballers this season, And was totally against anything approaching good play. The wearers of the myrtle green, however, kept their appointment with the lads of Oldham, and although the ground at that place was thoroughly unfit for play, both teams made the best of it, and the spectators were by no Maa. nor of means lacking pluck, for a large number of the lovers of the game assembled round the Enclosure. There was a strong and treacharoul Wiwi blowing at the time Ingham kicked off for Oldham. Runcorn immediately pressed, and Broady scored. The irrepressible Brazen- dale was equal to the occasion, and kicked a magnificent goal. This success on the part of the visitors appeared to awaken the Oldham team to the necessity of playing spiritedly and systematically, and after a rush down the field Moseley got in for Oldham; but the attempt at goal failed. Runcorn then obtained several minors, the result of the long kicking of Brazendale,the play beingin the home quarters. Johnson made a capital run to the visitors' line. H. Hughes kicked well and relieved, and the score registered at half-time was—Runcorn, 1 goal, 6 minors; Oldham, 1 try. On the resumption of play, Oldham showed better form, and a stubborn ifie:crmina- tion to equalize matters. The Runcornians dribbled tie ' ball to the home team's line, when a free kick afforded relief. Beetham obtained a try, which Broadbent con- verted into a goal, the result at the termination of play , , being—Oldham, 1 goal, 1 try, and 4 minors; Runcorn, 1 goal and 7 minors. WYCLIFFE v. ST. ELPHIN'S.—This match wa.s played on the ground of the latter on Saturday, before 200 specta- tors. Both teams were strongly represented. Cotton won the toss, and elected to play with the wind. Wycliffe soon settled down to their work, and scored a minor. The play was very even for a time, until Evans, receiving the ball at the half-way flag, made a dashing run in, Warton failing at goal. Myles dropped out, and a free kick was awarded to Wycliffe for off-side tackling, from which Walton almost landed a goal. Emmerson, Knowles, and Evans were next prominent for Wycliffe; the latter passed finely to Scott, who raced round his opponents in fine style and ran in at the corner flag. Warton again failed at the place. A long kick by Warton to Singleton resulted in the latter having his kick charged down by Emmerson; the same player getting hold put in a short run, and dropped the ball over the bar. Immediately after this Emmerson scored a try. Warton landing a goal. Half-time was called with the score—Wycliffe, 2-2--i; St. Elphin's, nothing. Re-starting, Evans was prominent with a run, and on being 'tackled passed to Brundrett, who succeeded in crossing the line with two of his opponents clinging to him. A maul ensued, the Wycliffe man finally having the best of it. Warton took the place, lint failed. Knowles was next to the fore with a spirited run, and gained a try, Williams failing at goal. Wycliffe con- tinued to press their opponents, and a loose scrimmage near the line resulted in Clayton getting over, Williams again failing at goal. St. Elphin's played up after this, and a free kick by Myles resulted in the ball going dead. Clegg was next to the fore with a good run, which ended in a try. Myles failed at goal. Time was now called, and Wycliffe retired the winners of a pleasant game by 2-5-3 to 0-1-1. Evans was the best back on the field, his running, kicking and passing being a treat to witness. He was ably assisted by Warton. Scott, Brundrett, Knowles, Cotton, and Emmerson. For St. Elphin's Sing,leon saved his side time after time, and Clegg, Gresty, and Myles were the pick. Referee, Mr. J. Hackett. WARRINGTON v. KENDAL HORNETS.

One of the most pleasant matches on the Warrington card was brought to an issue on Saturday, when the Hornets, of Kenilal renown, were met for the first time this season. It will be remembered that last season the Kendal team accounted for the Warringtonians in both matches, and with a remeaibrance of this fact, special endeavours were made by our local club to place their strongest team in the field. This was interefered with through the county having prior claims on W. Dillon's services, but otherwise a capital team journeyed to try conclusions with the premier Westmorland club. The outlook during the morning was not at all favourable to the match; but the storm cleared off towards noon, only to return with a more disastrous effect at the advertised time to kick off, viz., 2.45. A perfect hurri- cane prevailed, and at one time it was doubtful if the match would take place. However, both teams braved the storm, and a fair attendance, which would other- wise have been much larger, favoured the match.

Walker, the Hornets' captain, won the choice of ends. and Frank Turner started against a strong wind. No return was effected, and the first pack were in the home twenty-five. The first to show up were Speakman, Antrobns, and Barnes, who put in some neat transfers, and for awhile the Kendal defence was severely tested. The fine play of Walker relieved his side, and a spirited run by Massey was the means of placing the " wire- pullers "at their original position. This extraordinary form of the Warringtonians against such a strong wind

came in for rio small amount a praise, and their exer- tions almost had the desired effect, through a grand dribble, in which Fair, Turner and Unswerth played a prominent part. Walker stopped a smart rush of the visiting side; but try as the Kendal men would, they could not stop the Warringtoniana from keeping the oval in the home quarters. Bandies put in a smart dribble, and almost got over, until -Henderson get the oval away when the greatest odds seemed against him ' Armstrong was now to the fore withainart work, but he found his match in Jolley. Barnes was applauded for ' some excellent work, but Parsons, Ellwood, and Wilson, by smart rushes, placed the oval at the half-way tag% Give-and-take play followed, the visitors' forwards working like horses, each showing a determination that , deserved the highest praise. Nevins, Ashton, and Povey were applauded for their efforts, after which Massey scampered across the field, winding up with a sterling kick •into the Kendal quarters. An unfortunate occurrence now happened to the visiting side, for Jolley in executing some work, had - the misfortune to sprain his shoulder, this necessitating his imme- diate retirement from the field of play. This caused a re-arrangement of the backs. 'Nevins was transferred from the forwards to his old position at full back, whilst Evans came to Jolley's position at three- quarters. Evans and Walker exchanged kicks, and quick passing by the visiting backs was nentittlized by similar tactics on the part of Berry. Walker, and lender-. son. Walker was againthe stviour ef his side by a smart save of the Warrington van; but a grand pass from Barnes to Massey was missed, and Henderson rushing up forced Evans to concede the first minor, by compelling him to kick dead. Ashurst spoiled the reply to the drop- out, and itames intercepting a pass of Walkers intended for Armstrong, the ball was taken to the Kendal twenty- five, wherethe whistle sounded half-time, the score then reading a minor to -the credit of the home team. On resuming. Barnes first became prominent by a smart kick to thelialf •way flag. Henderson as promptly replied back again, but the Warringtonians, with the, assistance of the elements, again placed the homesters on their defence, and after Hine and Evans had exchanged kicks, the home team went away with a dash, and for a time the 'Warrington citadel was threatened. Walker, essayed& drop at goal, but only a minor resulted. The drop-out was only 'feebly responded to, and a good dribble by Wilkinson was checked in the nick of time by Antrobus. Walker now led his men in a smart rush, but Barnes was equal to the occassion, and taking the oval from the Kendal forwards' feet he punted grandly in touch at the half way flag. Evans following up well, and Hine securing possescion he threw the ball out, intending it for Armstrouk. Evans intercepted and galloped off at top speed, being knocked into touch close to the line. Bandies, however, was following up in the centre of the field, and Evans throwing the oval well out he placed the ball into Bandies' hands, who I grounded over the line with Henderson clinging to his neck. Barnes, however, failed at the place. This success of the visitors placed the Kendal men on their mettle, and soon after restarting Walker made a dashing run, being brought down by Massey. The last-named I eventually made his mark, but Hine responded. Pass- ing by the lfornet's backs almost ended in scoring, and a grand dribble by the Warrington forwards ended in Turner struggling over, but the point was disallowed. The game was now virtually over, and although the Hornets strove hard to obtain a foothold in the Warrington twenty-five, they failed to obtain a lead, and finally War- rington ran out the winners of a pleasantly contested game, by one try to Kendal Hornets two minors. ' Taking into account that the weather was sadly against a first-class display of football, it cannot be I denied that Saturday's contest was the best that has ever been witnessed between these two teams. The play was of the most interesting discription,.and it was pleasing to note the friendly spirit in which the match was conducted. Not a single hitch occurred during the whole of the game, but when it is said that Warrington were only playing 14 men the greater portion of the game, all the more credit is due to them for their victory. Special comment is out of the question,.and a marked improvement is noticeable with respect to the quick following up of the Warringtonians, a similiar remark applying to their tackling. On behalf of Kendal, Walker, Henderson, Ellwood, Parsons, and Wilson are deserving of praise. A SERIES OF ROBBERIES AT EARLESTOWN.

At the Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, a number of charges of theft were investigated by the magistrates! Michael Callighan and Abraham Appleton, boys, were brought up in custody on charge of having, on an .100 inst., and at other times during the past six monthe, stolen 31 wine glasses, 6 spirit glasses, nine glees tumblers, 3 glass jugs, 1 glass ornament. 1 glass sugar, basin. and 1 glass ffprer stand, the pro- perty of Thomas Walton, glass manufacturer, , Cross-lane, Newton. Mary Gibbons. Mary Callig- Omn, and Elizabeth Appleton, the two .latter the mothers of the male prisoners, were, ctarge4 with having received the articles, knowing them to have been stolen. Evidence *as, given by flir. Walton, who identified the glass. as his property, and said that the two lath who were 'accused of the theft had beenworking for him. P.C. Came* proved apprehending the prisoners. Mr. H. L. Riley, (St. Helens) appearedlor Mrs. Gibbons. Ind said that she purchased some ef the glass with no guilty knowledge, and more out of charity for the seller than anything else. After hearing evidence at considerable length the Bench decided to dismiss the ease as against Mrs. Gibbons. Michael Callighan was lined ss. and costs, or, in default of payment. 14 days' imprisonment. Abraham Appleton was similarly dealt With, and Mary Callighan and Elizabeth Appleton were each fined 10s, and costs, or, in default of payment, 14 days' imprisonment.—Edward Garnett, a youth, emploY-rtity Mr. Walton. was charged with having. on.j.be 21st October, stolen two glass bell ornaments, fronithe works of his employer at Newton. A witness was called to state that the prisoner made the glass bells for him, and Mr.-Walton said that as a matter of fact the pnisoner did make the ,bells himself, and might not think that he was stealing. It was pretty well understood that these things were taken, and they did not think much about it. He asked the magistrates to deal leniently with the case. A fine of ss. and costs, or I.* days' imprisonment in default, was imposed.— Daniel Whitty, of Alma-st. Earlestown, a boy of fourteen, was charged with having stolen four custard glasses from the works of Mr. Walton, on the 16th inst. Mr. Walton told the Bench that prisoner had been working for him for about a month, and added that most of the people employed at a glass works took something away with them. 'Mr. Houghton, whe presided on the Bench, said he thought there should be a notice put up in such works prohibiting the taking away of articles.—Mr. Walton: We do not allow it if we know it.—Mr. Houghton : It would have some effect if you put rap a notice. •I should try to stop the practice. —Mr. Walton said lie thought that those prosecutions would go a long,w,ay .towards stopping it.—The Bench imposed a fine;ef .Ss. and costs, or 14 days in default of payment. Two .boys, named Edward Bailey and John Joseph Mole, were charged with having stolen six meat pies' the property of Richard Griffiths, of 14, Grafton- st., Earlestown. John Griffiths, a lad, the son of the owner of the pies, was carrying them on a tin, that was placed on his beadrorhen the prisoners came up, took six pies off the tin, and ran away. They afterwards admitted having committed the offence, aid expressed contrition for it. .Bailey was sent to prison for 14 days, and Mole was fined 25,„ 6d. and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment in default of payment.—Alfred Morgan, an inmate of the Newtonitefornaatory School, pleaded guilty to a charge of haying stolen mx milk cakes from the shop of Thomas Wharton, 1.4, Queen-st., Earlestorm, on the 15th inst.—He was hauled over to the School authorities for punishment.

A NORTON FARAFER AND 1118 DEAD COW. On Monday, at the Runcorn Petty Sessions, before Mr. Charles Reynolds and Major Hazlehurst, Charles , Percival, of Hindley Wood Farm, Norton, WAS stun- mened by the Rimeorn Rural Sanitary Authority, I for being in possession of the carcase of a cow, which was unfit for the food of man, and which was prepared for sale and intended for the food of man. —Mr. W. H. Linaker prosecuted and Mr. A. Fletcher defended.—Mr. Linaker stated that on Monday the 12th inst., Sergeant Jones saw the defendant's milk cart, being driven trom Sutton Weaver Station. The servant of Mr. Booth, butcher, Runcorn. WAS an occupant of the cart. Having heard previously that defendant had on his premises a cmy that was ill, his suspicions were aroused, and during the night he visited the defendant's farm. In a shed he found the carcase of a cow, which was dressed in the ordinary way 1 as if for sale. He communicated with Mr. karrington, the sanitary inspector, and on Tuesday morning they wont to the farm together. Afterwards Dr. Adams, medial officer to the Union, examined the carcase, and condemned it as unfit for human food, and it was after- wards deetroved on the order of Mr. Chadwick, a magis- trate.—P.S. Imes deposed that on Tuesday morning, he asked the defendant if he intended to sell the meat for ' human food and he reviled "Yes I intend to make the best of it." Mr. Farrington then asked "Have you made any arrangement with Mr. Booth for the carcase"; Defendant said "No, I intend to sell it myself."—By Mr. Fletcher : After this conversation Mr. Farrington said, he was going to report it to the medical officer, and the defen- dant remarked, "Yes, if it is passed, I will sell it any- body." Mr. Bate, veterinary surgeon, said he thought the meat was good food.—lnspector Farrington admitted that the defendant had said he intended to make the , best of the cow if it was passed. This was after he had I arranged for the medical officer to inspect the carcase. There was no attempt at secresy. The carcase was in an open shed. The entrails, &c., were preserved in a hamper. Mr. Fletcher amid laughter, asked if the cow had been "killed to save its life."—Dr. Adams des- cribed the condition of the carcase and the various organs, and said it was unfit for human food.—Mr. Fletcher for the defence, said the cow was intended for the food of man only had it been passed by some compe- tent authority. The defendant had behaved in the most straightforward and open manner, and had it been intended to seed the carcase to market, nothing would have been easier.—Thomas Bate, veterinary surgeon, said he was (Ailed to see the cow after it had calved and on his advice the cow was afterwards slaughtered. The carcase was a fairly healthy one, but the lungs and liver were affected a little. He had arranged with Mr. Per- cival to examine the carcase on the morning of Tuesday. —Levi Knowles, in the employ of Mr. Booth, butcher, said he killed the cow in the ordinary way and he was told to leave it until next morning until Mr. Bate had examined it.—Mr. Reynolds said that so far an the Bench cqukl judge, the defendant had acted with perfect bona fides, but they could not in any way approve of the tactics of what was commonly called killing the animal to save its life. The Sanitary Authority had acted with great promptitude, and had taken a very proper course; but upon the evidence the Bench consiciered themselves justified in dismissing the case.

WARRINGTON FARMERS' CLUB. COUNTY COUNCIL CANDHPATES. An adjourned special general meeting of the members of the Warrington Farmers' Club, to which all persons interested in agriculture were I invited, was held on Wednesday evening, at the Corn Exchange, Warrington, its special object being to consider the se.ection of candidates to represent the interests of owners of land, tenant farmers, and farm labourers, in the County Councils. The chair was occupied by Mr. George Percival, Presi- dent of the club. After a preliminary statement I by the chairman, the meeting proceeded to select candidates for the various electoral divisions embraced in the area of the club's membership, as follows APPLEToN.—Mr. Wre-Bradford (Reddish Hall) proposed that Mr. Joseph Knowles (Appleton), a .member of the club, be the candidate for the electoral division of Appleton, near Warrington. In seconding this resolution, Mr. T. Dutton (Newton-by-Daresbury). said that he hoped the farmers ot the division would return Mr. Knowles by a large majority to the County Council. Mr. Knowles had had large experience in local board affairs, and he (the speaker) did not think there- was in . the division a•person more suitable to represent it. The proposition, having been supported by Mr. John Derby- shire (Stratton) and Mr. W. Derbyshire (Morris Brook), was unanimously carried. The nomination was accepted by Mr. Knowles. DARESBORY.-Mr. William Whitlow (Preston Brook) proposed that Mr. Henry Nield, J.P., of Higher Whitley, be selected as the candidate for the Daresbury division of Cheshire. Mr. Nield had, he said, been a farmer all his life, and was a suitable person to look after the wants of the farmers. The motion was seconded by Mr. T. Dutton (Newton-by-Daresbury), and carried, a proposition from the chairman that Mr. Henry Linaker, of Prodsham, clerk to the Runcorn Board of Guardians, be selected, not receiving a seconder. Bownow.—On the proposition of Mr. Pearson (Dunham), seconded by Mr. Davies (Hollinfare), it was resolved to ask Mr. W. Henry Heywood, of Bowdon, to I stand as candidate for the Bowdon division.

KNOTSFORD.—.Mr. Davies (Hollinfare) proposed that Mr. Hough, of Meie, be. nominated as the candidate for the Knutsford electoral division, a suggestion which was seconded by Mr. John Derbyshire (Stretton). Mr. Hough remarked that, now agriculturists had the privi- lege of having a voice in the spending of their own money, they should be prepared to take advantage of it. He thought that action might have been taken earlier than had been the ease with very good results. H 4 was 'afraid that a large proportion of magistrates would be elected to the County Couitcils, and that they would afterwards elect magistrates as aldermen, so that in the end there would perhaps be very little change in the matter of representation. The proposition was carried. LYMIL-Mr. Hough (Mere) then proposed that Mr. Richard Dutton (Lymm), a member of the Knutsford Board of Guardians and the Lymm Local Board, be chosen as a candidate for the electoral division of Lynam. The proposition was seconded by Mr. Davies (Hollinfare.) Itts an alternative motion, the name of Mr. J. L. Stelfox (Lymm), the honorary secretary of the club, was put before the meeting, on the proposition of Mr. W. Derbyshire (Morris Brook), seconded by Mr. John Derbyshire (Stretton), and supported by Mr. A. Barber (Whitley), and by the chairman. Oa a vote being taken, Mr. Stelfox received a majority of one, and it was thus decided to ask him to accept nornina. tion.

WINWICK. —Mr. William Darbyshire proposed that Mr. James Warburton, of DaHam, be nominated as a candi- date for the Winwick Division of Lancashire, which was agreed to. The meeting was then adjourned, it being decided to ask the candidate to meet the members of the club at the next meeting, to ascertain their views in regard to the matter.
PRESCOT.

STEALING • DOLLY Tun.—At thePrescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, John Sherwood, a glassblower, of St. Helens, was charged with stealing a dolly tub, valued at 6r. 6d., the property of William Brown, of Giller's Green, oe Saturday night. He was fined 205., or in default of payment, a month's imprisonment. CART ACCIDENT.---On Wednesday afternoon a cart belonging to Mr. W. Thompson of St. Helens in charge of John Kenny, was going down West-st., when the weight of the load broke the front board. This it is thought, caused the horse to take fright, the animal at a good rate as far as Whittaker's gate, where a wheel came off the cart. The horse fell, and the cart and its contents were seriously damaged. CHUB.= OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETT.—The fourth entertainment of the season, in connection with the Prescot branch, was held in the Houghtoa-street schoolroom, on Monday, when the chair was taken by the vicar, the Rev. H. Mitchell, during whose temporary absence the Rev. D. H. Stubbs succeeded. The room was crowded. Mr. G. D. F. Stephens of Liverpool gave an interesting address. Three pledges were taken during the evening. The programme was well rendered by Misses Brandreth (who officiated as the accompanist), Kate Keefe, Rose Keefe, Mr. S. Ames, Mr. J. Heaps and party. Gild& TRESPASS : HEAVY PENALTY.—At the Preseot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, William Winstanley, collier, Thatto Heath, and Henry Newton,. collier, St. Helens, were charged with trespassing in search of game, on land at Ecaleston, in the occupation of Mr. Richard Appleton, farmer, and belonging to the Earl of Derby. Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared to prosecute, and Mr. H. L. Riley defended. It appeared that on the 19th October the prisoners were seen on the land with a net in their possession and a hare was caught. The defence was a denial of the charge and Mr. Riley submitted that the evidence for the prosecution was of a very weak character.—Newton was fined 20s. and costs, and Winstanley, who had been previously convicted for highway robbery and poaching, was lined £5 and costs; or in default Of payment, two months' impzison- meat. The prisoner Winstanley exclaimed: You are sending me as innocent as a new-born child this minute.
AS ELOPEMENT AT RIINCORN.-A FOR-

- - - -- • GIVING HUSBAND. Before Mr. Charles Reynolds and Major Hasle- burst, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday. a young man named Thomas Angels, an electrician, and Phoebe Powell, were charged under a warrant, with having, on the 7th Nov., stolen ,a sewing machine, two blankets, two sheets, and a number of other articles, 'the property. of William Henry Towel', chemical labourer, Bentinck-st., husband of the female prisoner.—Mr. W. H. Linaker, solicitor, said he was instructed by the prosecutor to with- draw the charge against the woman, with the con- sent of the Bench. He was quite satisfied to take his wife back, forgive her what she had done,, and not refer in the future to what had taken place within the last few days. The prisoner Angels had been a lodger at the house of the prosecutor, who was convinced he had overpersuaded the wife to elope with him and take part of the furniture. Per the sake of himself and wife, and the family of three children, the husband hoped the Bench would set the woman at liberty.—Superintendent , Hollingworth said he did not see how it was possible to ' separate the cases; and before the police could consent to a withdrawal at all the costs incurred, amounting to £5 7s. 2d., must be paid. The, prisoners were traced.to 'Hull, and then were apprehended by Inspector O'Donnell. —Mr. Linaker said the male prisonet was to blame, and ought to take the responsibility.—Mr. Reynolds said they were advised by the Clerk, that if they heard one case, they must hear both.—After a conversation with his clients, Mr. Linaker said he was willing to' withdraw, from both eases and , pay the costs, for the sake of the wife.—Mr. Reynolds said it was a question whether' in the interests of domestic happiness, they could allowt he cases to be withdrawn. He thought . himself that the husband was behaving uncommonly well.—Mr. Linaker said the husband put the law in motion, and he wished to stop it.—Superintendent Hollingworth did not now oppose the withdrawal, and the Bench set the prisoners at liberty.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

Lancashire scored another decisive victory on Satur- day, their opponents on this occasion being the county representatives of Northumberland. The game took place on the Jesmond ground, Newcastle. The half- time score was—Northumberland, two goals; Lanca- shire, three tries, the home team hying been much helped by a strong wind. In the second half the Lanca- shire players held the upper hand completely and ran out winners by five goals, four tries and one minor to Northumberland two goals. W. Dillon, the captain of the Warrington team, formed one of the winning team. In the match Lancashire v. Yorkshire, to be played at Whalley Range, Manchester, to-day. the following teams have been selected York- shire : J. Dodd (Halifax), back ; P. Robertshaw , (Bradford), J. W. Sutcliffe (Fleckmondwike), and R. E. Lockwood (Dewsbury), three-quarters; W. Stadden (Dewsbury), and F. Bonsor (Bradford), half backs ; L. Hickson, J. Toothill (Bradford), F. Lowrie. J. H. Jones (Wakeeeld Trinity), H. Bedford (Morley), H. Wilkinson (Halifax), D. Jewett (Hecknsondwike) T. Else (Batley), and G. Jacketts (Hull), forwards. Lancashire :A. Hoyle , (Broughton Rangers), back; J. Valentine (Swinton), A. H. Molesworth (Manchester), and J. Standring (Man- chester), three-quarter backs • J. Mills (Swinton), and J. H. Payne (Broughton), half backs; C. Anderton (Free Wanderers). H. Hasleham (Manchester Rangers), W. Dillon (Warrington), H. C. Chapman (Old Boys), J. E. Or (Manchester), J. Strang (Liverpool), H. Eagles (Salford), E. J. Green (Manchester), and J. Woodward (Tyldesley), forwards. The Lancashire team is identical with that chosen to play against Northumberland last week, with the exception that H. Eagles (Salford) fills the place of Whittaker (Manchester). Misfortunes never come singly, and Runcorn, after a singularly successful season, sustained a double defeat on Saturday. At Oldham the first team were van- quished by the organization of that town, and the second Warn fared no better at home. The reverse was all the more galling to the first team because Oldham had I not previously this season managed to score a win, and that a few weeks ago Oldham had had to cry" enough" to Widnes. The winning point was only scored a few moments before the call of time, and then from a pass that was palpably thrown forward several yards. How- ever, the referee allowed die point, and there was sorrowing in the camp of the Cheshire Champions. It is worth mentioning that both those sterling forwards, Wainwright and Faulkner, were absent. This defeat has caused considerable alterations to be made in the team to-day, when Rochdale Hornets pay a visit to Runcorn. Brazendale will occupy his usual place at full back, and W. A. Riley will again do duty on the wing, but Woods will take the place of Cromp- ton at centre, and Wainwright will replace Davies on the wing. It is thought that a rest will do " Tommy" good. Another important change is the substitution of W. Hughes for Hollingworth at half back. The vacancies in the forwards will be filled up from the second team. It is rather a hazardous proceeding to reorganize the team when a club with the reputation of the Hornets has to be faced, but the best results are anticipated. . _ . .

_ Widnes had hard lines in meeting defeat a the hands of the Manchester Rangers, on Saturday. The Chemicals had much the best of the game, and victory appeared within their grasp until the last few minutes, when the Rangers pushed the ball over the line, and scored a try from which the premier point was added. Of course, as usual, when playing away from town Widnes were far from being well represented, and the result does not look creditable, when placed besides the crushing defeat they inflicted upon a Swinton team the week previous, and better things ought to be accomplished.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

On Thursday forenoon fortnightly meeting of the members of the Prescot Board of . Guardians was held at the Workhouse, Whiston. Mr. J. Kenwright occu- pied the chair. WORKHOUSE INN.ArEs.—Mr. Hale, master of the work- house, reported that there were 562 persons in the workhouse this week, 583 last week, and 534 in the corresponding week last year. There had been 53 vagrants relieved during the week, against 55 in the corresponding week last year. RAILWAY ACCIDENT TO Two Nrusxs.—At a meeting of the Visiting Committee, the master reported that Nurses Whitfield and Probert had been confined to their rooms, in consequence of injuries sustained whilst travelling by the London and North-Western Railway from Liver- pool to Prescot on that date. It was resolved that two nurses be engaged from the Nurses' Institute, Ashton- street, Liverpool, until they are able to resume their duties. The railway cempany had written admitting liability for the injuries sustained by Miss Roberts and Miss Whitfield, but were not responsible for consequen- tial damage. The Clerk was instructed to ask the company to re-imburse the guardians for the extra cost incurred by the ratepayers. Glsrs.--A vote of thanks was passed to Miss Frank, of Liverpool, for the gift of a parcel of papers, for the use of the inmates, and Mr. Leatherbarrow expressed a wish that the gentry of the neighbourhood would send gifts of flowers. . AN A PPOINTMENT.-Mr. R. G. Waterman was appointed school attendance officer, and school fees officer, for the Woolton district. _ _

FINANCIAL QUESTIONS—Mr. Johnson + moved that no subject which may involve any expenditure of £3O or upwards be introduced until the f ull Board has been previously advised. Mr. Graves seconded the motion.— In the course of a discussion which followed it was stated that the standing orders provided that any proposed expenditure, beyond the weekly payments, of amounts over £lO should be notified to the members, and the motion was defeated by a large majority. THS Sr. HELENS CORPORATION AND THE GUARDIANS.— The Clerk reported that he had beem in communication with the St. Helens Corporation in reference to the recep- tion of pauper cases in their hospital and he thought the Corporation were prepared to accept an annual sum, without actually making the patients paupers.—Mr. Lowe gave notice that at the next meeting he would move that the sum of £4O per annum be offered the Corporation to receive 'pauper cases from St. Helens in their hospital.—This concluded the business.

FACTORY FIRB.—Two LIVES LOST.—Two men, one Thomas Moore, the other not identified, lost their lives at the works of Storey Brothers, Lancaster, on Thursday forenoon. Whilst the men were working in the towell- ing department the oilcloth passing through the machine suddenly ignited, and the flame shot down like lighten- ing to the rooms below. The whole was soon in a blaze. Twelve jets of water were set to work, but the building was completely gutted.. Moore and another man were found amongst the debris, one quite unrecognizable. The damage to material and building is heavy.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD:
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD:

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday. Mr. T. S. Timmia presided and there were present the Rev. Dean Finegan, Rev. Father Clarke, Major Waring, Messrs. Deacon, Davies. Imi- son, Barlow, Heyes, and Dr. O'Keeffe, with Denby (clerk).

div.head: DISTRICT EDUCATION.
div.p: DISTRICT EDUCATION.

The District Education Committee reported that during October there were 154 applications for payment of fees, which were recommended to be paid in 136 cases. There were 191 parents summoned before the Committee for contravention of the Education Act; 43 were sum- moned before the magistrates and 39 convicted. Two boys were sent to an Industrial School.
A YEAR'S WORE

Mr. H. Wade Deacon presented a report of the work of the District Education Committee during the past year ended August 31st., 1888. The abstract of figures showed that there were 3,865 cases summoned before the Com- mittee, previous year 4,289 ; persons 1,440, previous year 2,116; for offences 2,308, previous year 2,686; persons 964, previous year 1,320; applications for payment of school fees 1,557, previous year 1,603; persons 476, previous year 798 ; fees recommended for payment (cases) 1,413, previous year 1,453; persons 352, previous year 650; prosecutions before the magistrates 611, previous year 352 fined ss. including costs 594, previous year 342; withdrawn 11, previous year 2; committed to Industrial Schools 6, previous year 8; children in Industrial School 42, previous year 39; average number of children on rolls 6,370, previous year 6,223.6 ; average attendance 5,352-5, previous year 50522; per centage 84.0, previous year 81.1.—Mr. Deacon, in moving the adoption of the report, alluded to the great increase in the number of prosecutions. He explained that it was owing to the fact that the attendance officers had visited the schools more frequently. The Committee were very chary about sending children to Industrial Schools, partly because it was bad for the parents to get rid of their children so easily, and because the taxpayers had to support these children. Alluding to the improve- ment in the. average attendance, Mr. Deacon said he did not know whether it was due to the increased severity ofithe Committee hi proseeuting parents. In former years they had had a large number of prosecutions, but they had not always been successful in getting a good attendance. He thought the result during the past year had justified the means. When a case was extremely bad, the attendance officers had authority to take it before the magistrates once a fort- night, if there was no improvement in the attendance. There were 15 names on the list, and in some of the cases there had been a marked improvement, and several names had been taken off the list. During the past year one person had been fined 15 times, another 14 times, and others 13, 11, and 10 times. These bad cases had a very bad influence upon the average attendance of a school, but, while the average attend- ance for the United Kingdom was 76.5 per cent., it was 84 per cent. in Widnes ; this was only to be expected as they were a town population. Dean Finegan pointed out that during the past year about £l5O was paid by parents who had been before the magistrates. Only one tenth of this sum was actually fines, whilst the other nine tenths went in costa to the county. It was time that something was done in this matter. The report was adopted and, on the motion of the Chairman, a vote of thanks was passed to the Committee.
FINANCE.
On the recommendation of the Finance Committee accounts amounting to £2,888 Is. 11d, were passed for payment. The receipts for the month amounted to £1,634 15s. ed.
GOTBRNMHNT GRANTS.

The Clerk read the reports of H.M. Inspector on the Board Schools, and stated that the total amount of gtsut earned at Simm's Cross School was £1.306 75. 4d. The sum of £157 3s. sd.had been deducted becausethe money spent *n the school did not equal the grant. At War- rington-road the grant amounted to £512 Bs. 4d., and at West Bank to £952 15s. 11d.—The Chairman said the deduction at Simm's Cross School was a tax upon the efficiency and economy of the school.—The reports were referred to the School Management Committee.
TEE SALE OP_ DRINK ON SUNDAY'.

• The Society for stopping the sale of Intoxicating Liquors on Sundays forwarded a petition in favour of this cause for signature by the Board.--The Chairman said this opened a wide question.—Dean Finegan remarked that if public houses were closed on Sundays there was no doubt that children would attend school more regularly on Monday mornings.—The Chairman did not think it was a question for discussion at a School Board, and he proposed that the petition lie on the table. —Mr. Heyes seconded the proposition, which was carried.
INDUSTRIAL SCHOOLS. A memorial from the Manchester school Board, with regard to industrial schools, was referred to the Educa- tion Committee. There was no other business of public interest.

Hard- man had been employed at Messrs. Pilkington's works, and filled up his spare evenings by billiard marking at the Wellington Hotel, St. Helens. The petition was forwarded to the Home Secretary, who handed it to the Commander-in-Chief for consideration, and Mr. Burchall has received a reply, of which the following is a copy : "I am directed by the Commander-in-Chief to acquaint , you that his Royal Highness has carefully considered the petitions addressed to the Secretary of State for the Home Department on behalf of Private E. While his Royal Highness does not refuse to hold out some hope of a portion of his sentence of 20 years' penal servitude being remitted at some future date, it will not be possible to consider the question for some years to come.—lpm, sir, your obedient servant, W Loscelles, Ad.
