Fairclough, C. P. Price. Clarke, KI Chidla.w, A. Woods, Sutton, Greener, C. Leigh,' and C. Jones. Mr. Woods, ably officiated as accotm

RHYMES IN TFfE DIALECT. • BROS.S.EN BILL. When Brossen Bill 'listed th' Fleece, He fancied blasel summat nobbv, An' swaggered,-_a guardian o' th' peace, Or, puttin' id plainly,—a Bobby! Wi' his buttons, an' suit o' dark blue, Fancy cap, an' a belt, black an' sbinin', He looked wee!, when he'd nowt mitch to do, Ageon a wo graceful reclinin'. Heaw he leered at young wimmin th' streets An' cooarted wi' servants up lobbies; For he liked wod wur tasty an' sweet,— Hey! rapput pie's relished bi Bobbies! He never refused a chop Heaw he gloried i' ale or cowd mutton! Nooon liked rood meyt better than Bill, But, then, nobry co'd him a glutton. Heaw th' lads chaffed him o'er his mita shoon, They wur just abeawt size ov a wisket ; His nooase, like a rooasey i' June, Looked fresh as beef cuttin's fro' t' brisket. He're pratty, to judge bi th' neat way He kept his wire moustache i' order, But lasses sed, regular away, His beauty wur in a black border!

It's mony a year neaw sin he trod Wi' stately march—trampin' on duty; Runnin' raskuls at times into " quod," An' kecpin' his een wide for beauty. But two or three antics wur played— Bill o'er his bowd deeds wur a bragger,— As ined William feel a bit fl iyed. An' rubbed o th' keen edge off his swagger.

For o he wur brossen an' big, He managed to drop o' odd cases Th' rough lads played him mony a "rig," As med him poo o sooarts o' faces. His mates i' th' fooarce gloried i' fun : 'Twur gam, an' they fair shook wi' laffin', Every time gumshus Billy geet "done." He welly went wild thro' ther' chaffin'.

One day, a lad snidged to his side, An' axed t' time o' day, varra quately. Bill drew his big verge eawt wi' pride, "It's twenty to one," he growled stately. Th' lad grinned an' bawled eawt "When its one Ged thi hevd shaved !" an' off quick he darted. Billy tried to nab th' urchin,—he'd gone! So he stood, puffed i' th' wind, an sad.hearted• As he stood theer, wi' booath eon ablaze, Another o' t' fooarce coom up gaily. "What's up, Bill ?" he sed, " hes't' a case ?" Bill towd him his tale. " Well! well! raylee !" He sed, as he looked at his watch, " I'th' oppen street, tha'rt med a foo on. But then, tek thi time, an' dornd fratch ; Tha's ten minutes good yet to do on !" Later on, when he'd getten mooar fawse At recknin' up dodges an' shammin', A bullock at slaughter broosk loce, An' sorabry sed, " Do stop thad gammin' ! Reawnd t' corner ther's tooathry, agate." Off Bill went to nab 'em at tossin'. The bull coom at a terrible rate, An' Bill he went scarlet wi' cossin'. He wur sucked in ageon woss than thad. " Ther's a 'bus just gone o'er !" sombry sheavrted• Billy wobbled away, heigh go mad For t' truth o' thad news he ne'er deawted. When he geet up to th' place he'd bin towd,— 'Twur th' brig,—he inquired, puffin rarish, The; geet anserd, an' fun he wur "sowd. "Ay, th' bus went o'er theer—to Church Parish •

Billy dreamt abeawt stripes on his arm, An' promotion, be tried hard to plan id ; But th' gret " suck " ov o wur too warm For a mortal like Billy to stan' id. Bill wur on his beeat, calmly at eeose, • When a chap put an end to his !Asses, He rushed up an' sod, " Pleecemon, do pleos Stop you chap fro' murtherin' his missus!" Wod! Wheer?" Billy sed, startin' up. " Whoa is id? Come, come, tell me further," t$ ! chap wagged his heyd like an' owd tup, "Hey, pleeeemon, it's reight wilful ,murther Billy's hair rooase an' lifted his hat; ".r Tho' help i' this case wur so urgent, He thowt, while be frothed in a swat, "

He'd better ged help off his Sargent. He whistled, an' two or three pleece Run up to brave Billy's assistance. Bill towd 'em and wi' staves apeice They fooarCed thro' o t' gret creawd's resistance' A woman wur kilt sure enuff, An' t' pleecemen o brasted laffter, 'rwur a show. Punch hed gi'en Judy snuff Bill left th' fooarce for ev(r soon after. Jecx o' Ateis• The sale of the Great Eastern, asbroken up, has so 0 realized £50,000. A.RRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

Thg fortnightly meeting of this Board of `ardians was held at the Workhouse on Wednes- ' morning. The Rev. G. F. Roberts presided, and .re were also present Messrs. Blackhurst, T. Jones, 4.. Roughton, Isherwood, Clarke, J. Houghton, Rat- Ole, Greening, Eckersley, Wright, D. Jones, Bal- -arrY, Darbyshire, Jolley; J. C. Sutton, (clerk) ; S. ton (assistant clerk) ; C. H. Ward, (Workhouse ter); and 11. M. Mines (superintendent of Pad- Schools.) COST OF RELIEF AT NEWTON. answerto Mr. Ratcliffe tile CLERK said the amount ',ended in relief at Newton was £l9 per week twelve

Ails ago, and it was about the same now. ' HOUSE COMMITTEE.—STONES AND STONE-BREAKING. Ilia Committee recommended that the broken stone the workhouse grounds be sold to the Corporation t 7s- I3d. per ton for 750 tons. The minutes also orded a letter in which the Borough Surveyor "titnated that the Paving and Sewerage Committee had nted the offer, and that they should commence to -,ave them shortly. The Committee also instructed Z! Workhouse matron to buy fruit for the Chrismas GrREENING, in moving the confirmation of e minutes, said the quantity of fruit this year was the 7Me as that of last year with the exception of 281bs. of Llirrants less. The total amount was a very great deal than it used to be—about one half he believed. Ijll-(r. ISHERWOOD seconded the proposal.—Mr. 201BYsHins said he was pleased that an arrange- ktent had been entered into with the Corporation to 2 the sale of the stones. He noticed that some of the one laid down by the Corporation between Warring- and Latchford was not half broken. Some of stones were as big as the glass on the table and some ir small as his little finger. If a road was to wear well t,l3e, stones should be as uniform as possible. He h,°K some of the stones home and compared them with ;,•"e stones on the new road made by .the shin Canal •_o,iitractor and found that they were not to be compared l'.llth:each other. He brought one of the stones there to show 47 the Board the difference between the stone they broke tio:l9. that used by the Corporation. He took the trouble 'or %quire where the Corporation stones came from and he told that they came from Ireland, and he believed tlkt the cost of carriage, &c., brought the sum total of to !ll' cost to a higher price than that Board were willing th 'Ake for the stone they had to dispose of. He thought cne bargain that had been entered into would benefit the orPoration as much as that Board.—Mr. GREENING said Ze,Was inclined to believe that the cost of the stone Lerred to by Mr. Darbyshlre cost the Corporation omewhat less than 7s. 6d. per ton —Mr. JOLLEY asked ;.f the matter of the Christnias dinner would again come ▪ fore the Board B—Mr. GREENING said it would.—Mr. *Mazy said he would be prepared to propOse a. modified Lllggestion as to the dinner. He should suggest that '4e females have half-a-pint of beer to their dinner. --Mr. GREENING objected to this matter being discussed Zt Present. There would, he said, be . nothing done in a ,?le-and-corner fashion.—The CHAIRMAN said the matter wag not on the minutes and could not be discussed then, the subject dropped.—The minutes of the House 'mrnittee were then confirmed. • APPOINTMENT OF SCHOOLMISTRESS. u.''he Pad gate Schools Committee recommended that Mary Keay, of Manchester, be appointed school- tress at Padgate schools at £3O per annum, with fticms and furnished apartments. The minutes were —"Armed.
I , 'ern°,
SCHOOL FEES. Ihis Committ.e, reported that fees had been allowed 53 cases 51 of which were old and 2 new !eases.— * the motion of Mr. Blackhurst the minutes were %4firmed.

GIFTS TO THE INMATES. In the Master's journal it was stated that the Platron wished to thank Mr. Jolley for a number of ~..`Graphies " and other illustrated papers ; and Mr. James narburton. jun., for a present of pictures. RELIEF AT EARLESTOWN. • b. The CLERK read a recommendation from the Newton ef Committee that Mr. Caldwell, the relieving 17""cer be instructed to call at Earlestown to dispense "ef on Thursday mornings on his way to Haydock.— hhe CHAIRMAN moved and Mr. GREENING seconded a toPosai that the recommendation be adopted, and this "as agreed tO. THE PROPOSED EXTENSION OF THE WORItHOUSE. . A letter was read from the Local Government Board .11cluiring as to what acton was being taken with ward to the proposed extension of the workhouse, d asking that the plans should be forwarded if corn- was decided that the Clerk should inform Local Government Board that the further considera- 'll3ll of the matter had been postponed for four months. GREENINV said the female side of the house was entirely full, as was also the hospital He hoped 709 should be able to do without an extension but he 4.1,3 r much feared they would not)—The CHAIRMAN ought that considering the time of the year and the Zr,eather they were doing very well.—The WORKHOUSE 'IAsTER said there were 327 inmates in the house, which as completely full in certain parts.—The matter then "roloped. THE sm.m OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS ON SUNDAY. A letter was read from the Secretary of the Central "Asociation for stopping the sale of intoxicating liquors "Dia Sunday, asking the Board to sign a petition to Parlia- Illent in favour of stopping the sale of intoxicating 41cl00rs on Sundays.—The CHAIRMAN said that when they "9 previously had that petition before them they had 4,9 opted it and he propsed that they should again adopt t'• He thought they should do all they could to check ,he miserable effects brought about by excess in drink- more especially on Sundays. Those who lived in (>l.lntry places and saw the Sunday desecrated by people ':>lning from large towns and drinking themselves into a Btate of helpless imbecility and generally setting a Wretched example to country people, who perhaps kight have no idea of conducting themselves in such a wax-, would surely sympa.hise with those who were Illakirg an effort to stop the sale of these liquors, at any ,!late on Sundays. (Hear, hear.) And, besides, it was ,r_otorious that there were innumerable other reasons Zily some course of that kind should be adopted.—Mr. *RBYSHIRE seconded the Chairman's proposal.—Mr. " • BOUGHTON was doubtful whether the signing of a Petition of that kind came properly within the province ‘.7.1 the Board.—Mr. GREENING was of opinion that that ,i,vkas the proper place for such a petition to be signed. I.l!eS knew something of drunkenness there and they 'lesk- something of it in the town. During the three or °Ur years that he had had a seat on the bench he was Illore and more convinced of the necessity of such a ?etition. The cases of drunkenness brought before the ,?,6•llch were of such a character and in such a quantity at if it were not for them they should have very little Tdeed to do. (Hear, hear).—lt was then agreed unani- tVously that the Chairman should sign the petition on half of the Board. This was all the business of public interest.

div.p: CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT WARRINGTON, A meeting of Conservatives of the North-East Ward was held in St. Peter's schoolroom, John-st., on Monday evening, for the transaction of annual business, and for the purpose of hearing an address delivered by Mr. James Croston„of the National Union, London. The chair was occupied by Coun- cillor Francomb, and there was a good attendance. ELECTION OF WARD CHAIRMAN. Mr. John Roberts proposed that Councillor R. W. Francomb be chairman of the Ward Committee for the ensuing year. They would all agree, he thought, that Mr. Francomb had done his work in such a manner that it could not be improved upon. Mr. Roberts then urged the Conservatives of the Ward to stick together, in order that they might always in future return Conservative candida•es to the Town Council. (Applause). —Mr. William Jolley, in seconding , the proposition, said that there was no one more fit to be chairman of the Ward Committee than Mr. Francomb, who was always ready with his assistance. Those were the sort of men they required. The resolution was then adopted unani- mously. MR. FRANCOMB ON SANITARY MATTERS. The Chairman, replying, said that whenever there had been an election there had been no difficulty in obtaining willing assistance. Up to the present they had never yet lacked help, and he believed that so long as they wanted helpers to return Sir Gilbert Greenall to the House of Commons, or to return any other good Conservative, they would have no difficulty whatever in getting that help. At the present time there were a lot of burning questions in Warrington. There was the question of the, depot in Lythgoe-s-lane, which was a very burning question to the people 'of that ward. For his own part, he was obliged to plead guilty to having taken some action in that matter. They knew very well that the difficulty of dealing with the excreta of a town was one that bothered not only Warrington, but other towns throughout the length and breadth of the United Kingdom. It was a very easy thing for people to take exception to the actions of .others, but it was a much more difficult thing for them to show what they would do themselves. They heard men getting upon platforms, and calling the system adopted in ‘Warrington, but they did not hear one of them say in what way that system might be remedied. He believed that the members of the Town Council—and especially the members of the Sanitary Committee—had not the slightest right to bring a nuisance to the door of any.man's house, but he was .quite certain that lip body of sensible' men would wish to stop progress if they could see any hopes that eyentually a sound determination would be arrived at. At the present moment they, had no less than 300 tons per week of excreta and ashes to deal with, and if they would only consider that 300 tons a Week meant 52 times that in a year, they would at once arrive at the conclusion that the Sanitary Committee had got plenty to do, and had a very difficult task before them. When they took 100 tons of tub contents to Longford they reduced it to seven tons of concentra- ted manure, so that they evaporated 93 per cent. of every- thing that went there. At the present moment they were actually making ten tons per week of concentrated i manure, which was n the open market worth at least £6 per ton. He believed that they Were on the right way, not only to get rid of the nuisance, but also to reduce the rates from the profits at Longford. He could quite see that the question of theintercepting depots was a 'difficult one. In the first place they must know that these places must be somewhere. The thing was to put them in the least objectionable places. He did not think that they were in the best places, but they were in the best that could be got at the time, and they were told distinctly that there wbuld be no nuisance He believed that the Sanitary Committee would do their utmost to see that there should be no nuisance. They only afked time. If, at the end of, say, another twelve months, things were not in a satisfactory state, he thought lomething should be done to remove the depots to another place altogether. If they knew how many people were continually coming to Warrington from other towns for information, they would find that War- rington was not the only place in which this difficulty was experienced. At one time, when they depended upon farmers to remove the manure from Longford, they had as much as 3,000 tons percolating into the earth, and polluting every stream of water in the neighbourhood. The farmers did not want the manure in summer, the time when it was most neceitsary that it should be got rid of, but in the spring and autumn. He was firmly convinced that they were on the right track, but he should certainly do all in his power to get any nuisance removed from the midst of the people in that ward, or any other ward. (Applause.) ELECTION OF OFFICERS &C. Mr. JAMES HILL moved, and it was resolved, that Colonel G. Y. Bolton, Councillor R. Heaton, and Mr. R. W. Collin be vice-chairmen ; that Mr. George Tolley be- honorary secretary ; that Messrs. Robert Bolton, W. P. Chorley, Richard Tickle, M. Chorley, Gilbert Lowe and William Strettle, be delegates to the Council ; and that the Captains 'of Division and Working Committee be the same as last year,, with power to add to their number." Mr. ROBEILT PIERPOINT moved "That this meeting expresses its unabated confidence in, and complete approval of, the policy of her Majesty's Government, particularly of the firm and humane 'manner in 'which the law has been administered in Ireland for the benefit of the country a.§. a whole and for the protection secured to the loyal portion of its inhabitants from the tyranny of the National League." (Applause.) Mr. JA,MES CROSTON seconded the resolution, which was carried, and delivered a political address. After- wards the meeting was brought to a close by the pass- ing of the usual votes of thanks.
RUNCORN AS IT IS AND AS IT OUGHT
TO BE.

The Hey. J. D. Thomas, pastor of Bethesda Congre- gational Chapel, Runcorn, concluded his series of discourses on this subject on Sunday evening, when he dealt with " Runcorn in relation to Public Worship, and Vital Religion." The preacher took for his text I Johnoic., 12v. "He that hath the Son hath life." Suppose said Mr. Thomas, in the course of his sermon, that someone from a distant land were to come and search for the Christian Faith in Runcorn, just as a botanist or zoologist went to foreign countries to collect rare plants and insects; did they think he would have much difficulty in finding it. He would observe certain buildings, whose architecture pointed them out unmistakeably as being devoted to religious purposes. They were not all equally pretentious. Some were very humble structures, and yet were centres of light in dark places. But taking them altogether, churches, chapels, and missions rooms, they number 19. The accommodation ranged from 1,300 down to 100; but the total accommodation would reach:about 11,000. On looking into the records of the town for the first quarter of the present century, the inquirer would find no more than three or four places of worship. And neither of these, excepting the Parish Church, was le any considerable size. So that during the intervening years much progress had been made in the provision for public worship. The provi- sion had kept pace tolerably well with the increase of population. Making due allowance for infants in arms, sick people, for the aged and infirm, there were not many more than 11,000 in the town who could reasonably be expected to attend the services of God's house. But progress was manifest, not only in the pro- vision for public worship, but also in the increase in adherents to the churches. And yet he was afraid that in this matter pace had not been kept with the increase of accommodation. There were often more sittings than worshippers. Still there had been a great increase even in the number of adherents during the past fifty or sixty years, and that was particularly noticeable with one community, viz., the Wesleyan Methodists. But do not let them imagine that religion consisted in handsome and commodious churches, and in the multiplication of societies. We might have all these and still not have a very strong sort of religion. "The stranger within our gates" in pur- suing his investigation, would pay particular attention to the mutual relations of the different com- munities. He would not expect to find them all embraced within one creed. Still remembering that believers in Christ were partakers of one divine nature, and that the religion of Christ was above all things a , religion of love, he would be more than disappointed if he did not. discover that the various denominations were

mutually helpful. Speaking from his own experience, he must say that there was a good deal of mutual help- fulness among the seven or eight branches of the great Church of Christ that existed in the town. It was shoWn in religious work and also in matters which demanded aid of a pecuniary nature. They could not say, and indeed it would be nothing short of a misfor- tune if it could be said, that they dwelt together in uniformity, but it can be said that to a large extent they "dwelt together in unity." So far he had put the bright side of the religious life of our town before them. Look at the proportion which their public assemblies bear to the accommodation. He I thought he was within the mark when he said that with the exception of four places (where the congregations were always good) their churches and chapels were rarely half filled. Look in the last place at the influence of the churches upon the masses. He had a pretty intimate acquaintance with the back streets and bye- ways, and on the strength of that acquaintance he hazarded the statement that considerably more than a quarter of the\ population of the town, rarely, if ever, enter a place of worship. This was unspeakably sad, and it did not say much for the power and vitality of their faith. They would lose a quarter, aid pay .hree- oence, sixpence,or a shilling,to witness a football match. They attended their benefit clubs and trade societies lint where were these meetings held. Not in the lecture halls or vestries of our chapels. They did not touch the people at any of these points. And why. Perhaps because their notions of Christianity had been too ethereal and unpractical. But chiefly because their faith had not the power over their own lives and hearts which it ought 4"to have. •

div.head: YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATIONS.
div.p: YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATIONS.

Sir,—l was pleased to see so many young men present at the meeting, which was held in Bewsey-street on Wednesday evening, to consider the desirability of forming in Warrington a Young Men's Christian Asso- ciation. There are over 4,000 branches in different parts of the world, and many are doing noble work in our large towns, especially in Manchester. lam sure there is a felt need in Warrington for such an association, where young men could meet together, for social and moral improvement ; it is needed as a counter attraction to the many places of amusement, which are doing their utmost to attract young men, and alas too often tend to demoralize rather than elevate the man. I hope all the ministers and gentlemen of the town, will support this scheme, and do their utmost to establish in Warrington a Young Men's Christian Association.—Yours &c., JOHN PATTERSON.

THE INCORPORATION OF WIDNES AND RUNCORN. Sir,—No doubt within the last few weeks you have noticed that sevoral towns, Chelmsford with 9,000 popu- lation, Loughborough 19,000 population, Workington 22,000 population, &c. have had the privilege of a Mayor and Corporation conferred on them. Now, in looking over some particulars of Lancashire, &c., I notice That the above two large towns are not incorporated ,although they are among the largest in the county without Mayors of their own. I suppose it only needs some one to take the matter up and work it with a will. I think you could in your paper break the ice on the matter, and educate and stimulate public opinion in the right direc- tion until the question was taken up by some of the prominent leading men in each of the above towns. Of course the thing will not be carried right off at once but by keeping pegging away at it, you will eventually attain your object. There is no doubt a Charter of Incorporation adds to the dignity and importance of a town, both in the eyes of its own townspeople and also in the opinion of the outside public at a distance. There is also the appointment of a Borough Bench of magis- trates, which is almost sure to flow from the grant of a Charter. I trust you will take this matter up with spirit and energy, and push it to a successful issue, so that it may not be many months before we hear of the elections of The first Mayor of Runcorn and Widnes.—Yours &c. T. N. G. P..—From a Parliamentary return it appears there are 121 municipal boroughs, with less than 10,000 popu- lation' so it will be very easy to make out a good case for each of the above towns.

div.head: FAULTY FOOTPATHS.
div.p: FAULTY FOOTPATHS.

Sir,—Allow me, through the medium of your columns, to call the attention of the Paving and Sewerage Com- mittee of the Corporation to the wretched state of the footpaths at the bottom of Bold-street. On wet days especially, the condition of the paths at the crossings opposite the Warrington Slate Company's Office is some- thing abominable, and I am sure the many ladies who have to pass this spot must often condemn the Com- mittee for their neglect of this well-frequented street. For myself, I am simply astonished that, considering, the number of town councillors who use this thorough- fare, attention has not been previously called to the unpaved and hooded state of this particular part of Bold-street. I would further venture to direct the Committee's attention to the road leading to the footpath over the iron bridge at Arpley. At the best of times the read resembles a swamp, but on and after wet days it is a 'complete quagmire. A still further matter 'Would like to point out is the abominable nuisance that has been Created at this foot bridge by the Erection of a couple of gates. Why they we erected, and what purpose they serve, I have teen unable to discover. If the erection oi the gates is the preliminary step to closing the road as a disused one it will soon be success- ful, for the intolerable nuisance of passing the gates is driving pedestrians, much against their will, round by Warrington Bridge. It is no sight on Sun- days, to see twenty or thirty persons waiting their turns at these gates, and the violent banging of them attests the hearty dislike of the passers-by. The gates them- selves are as narrow as they could well be made, and highly calculated to inflict injury upon any extra stout individual who essays to pass through. The odours that pervade these barricades is of so high a quality as to call for the attention of the Inspector of Nuisances ; and if the accumulation of excreta progresses at the hitherto steady rate the attendance of a Longford van will soon be necesso ry.—Yours truly, A SUFFERER.

div.head: "THE STOCKTON HEATH SWELLS AND THE SHOP ASSISTANT."
div.p: "THE STOCKTON HEATH SWELLS AND THE SHOP ASSISTANT."

Sir,—The bombastic epistle of your correspondent " Chivalry " (who, by the way, belies the on de plume he has chosen) is an apt illustration of the trite maxim "No case—abuse your opponent." Stripped of its abuse, the effusion of your correspondent presents the sorry spectacle of an emaciated skeleton whose bones crumble at the slightest touch. With reference to the stale platitude as to my "rushing into print," the "rushing" I did was indolence itself compared to the heedless impetuosity of your " innocent " correspon- dent. Really" Chivalry" writhes under my remarks as one who has been hit. _

As to my "facts," they stand where they did, and " Chivalry " is altogether unable to go behind them. With all his bumptious bravado, your correspondent, your readers will notice, does not attempt to deny a single one of them, but takes refuge in casting the onus , of answering my charge upon the Carriage Company, and in hiding himself amongst "some 20 involved." But I did not involve 20—I only referred to two. Judg- ing from "Chivalry's" remarks, I should have been wkollv annihilated by the thunderbolts of an indignant round-robin from this large company' of suspected characters, but singular t• state, not one of them feels aggrieved. Methinks, these 18 are holding their aching sides, after the mirth-provoking proceedings of your correspondent. He taunts me with "slinking under cowardly anonymity," and then, forsooth, goes and does the " slinking " trick himself! The letter of Mr. W. Russell is only part of a little whitewashing process, and does not help your correspon- dent " Chivalry " at all. Will either Mr. Russell or " Chivalry" deny (1) that a letter of complaint has been received on this subject ; (2) that the conductor narrowly escaped dismissal; (3) that the young lady has been stopped riding; and that " Chivalry " knows anyhing of tho letter ?—Yours, kc., A PASSENGER.

div.head: COUNCILLOR BOLTON AND THE WATCH COMMITTEE.
div.p: COUNCILLOR BOLTON AND THE WATCH COMMITTEE.

Sir,—And so at last, after a great amount of haggling, Councillor Bolton's ambition is gratified—he is now a member of the Watch Committee. Rumour says this is a position he has coveted for some time past for reasons of his own. It is, however, a source of some satisfaction to the town to know that this, as I think, improper appointment of the Town Council, was not made un- challenged; and personally I tender my thanks to the worth' few who resisted it so far as the rules and forms of business in the Council would allow. On one of the objectors—Councillor W. Pierpoint—this resistance brought insult from Councillor Bolton, that gentleman SO far forgetting himself, as well as the time and place, as to Five the "lie" to Councillor Pierpoint. And here, Mr. Editor, just let me say that not a few burgesses of the town are very much dissatisfied with the part our esteemed Mayor took in this unpleasant episode. Councillor Pierpoint did not receive that pro- tection at the hands of the Mayor he had a right to expect. In opposing the scandalous appointment of Councillor Bolton to the Watch Committee, Councillor W. Pierpoint was honestly performing an important public duty; he sought to protect the larger public interest, as against the smaller and personal one, and whilst so creditably engaged, most people will think, the Mayor—as the chairman and highest official of the Council—ought to have protected him from the insult- ing remark of Councillor Bolton in the most effectual manner possible, which unfortunately he neglected to do. Now, coming to the appointment of Councillor Bolton on the Watch Committee, I would ask, " Is it a wise thing to give s ats and votes on that committee to brewers, licensed victuallers, and others" largely inte- rested in the drink traffic of the town? What, think you, would be the answer our esteemed Chief Constable

would give if consulted on such a question? I feel sure he would much prefer a Watch Committee where brewers, Sic., were conspicuous by their absence. Councillor Bolton may be a perfect gentleman—his character,for aught I know,may be irreproachable—but, seeing that the trade with which he is closely asso- ciated is frequently concerned in matters brought be- fore the Watch Committee, for this reason it is better for the public interest he should not be a member of that committee. Had he been a sensitive and discerning matt he would not have sought such a position. The presence of men of Councillor Bolton's class upon the Watch Committee must always be a serious hindrance to the due and impartial performance of the duties imposed upon the officers of our police force. I submit that the difficulty of trying to serve two masters ought not to be created by our Town Council for our police officers. The greatest of living statesmen has said that the principle and object of all legislation should be to make it "easy to do right, and difficult to do wrong." I contend, Mr. Editor, that this sound and wise principle has been outraged in the appointment of Councillor Bolton on tke Watch Committee.—Yours, • ONE WHO HATES AXE GRINDING.

THE ENFORCEMENT OF THE LICENSING LAWS. Sir,—l have been interested in the letters which have appeared in your columns under the above heading, and, as the subject is one of very considerable public importance I should like to be allowed to say a few words about it. Mr. Chidlaw heads his letters with the very suggestive prefix "Coercion and teetotalism." This is a very catching phrase, and has done service on many a previous occasion. I should like to know what coercion was used towards Mr. Longton ? If Mr. Chid. law's view of the matter is right, then ever 7 attempt to exact a pledge on any subject from a candidate is coer- cion. Or does he mean that coercion consists in putting the law in force? Because, if he does, I am afraid that a good many people besides publicans will have an equal right to cry out about coercion. It is owing to coercion, i.e., the enforcement of the law, that we require police- men, magistrates, judges, prisons, and it is owing ta coercion that we fine, or send to prison, the poor man or woman who hasbroken the law by getting drunk. And if a publican breaks the law—as he undoubtedly does when he makes a man or woman drunk—then why should he not have a taste of this same coercion? For the life of me, I know of no reason why he should not. I see no reason why publicans, any more than other peo- ple, should be superior to the law. Mr. Chidlaw asks if the existence of a respectable body of men is to be made miserable by persecution, i.e., by coercion, i.e., by the enforcement of the law. Well, sir. certain other classes of law-breakers—whose breaches of the law have not a tithe of the evil consequences to the public that those of publicans have—complain that their lives are made miserable—that they are driven from place to place—from pillar to post, by the police. lam not surprised that Mr. Chidlaw is not "amused." It would be rather too much to expect him to be, . .

Now as to the restrictions put upon "the trade." Take such a case as he mentions of a drunken man gain- ing admission to licensed premises. Well, I suppose the man had been made drunk at some other public house, and if the publican on whose premises he was found had not supplied him with drink, then it would be the duty of the police to find out where he had been supplied. But such reasoning as this of Mr. Chidlaw's I consider to be the veriest trifling, for such a case as he mentions is a very extreme one. I have, not once, but scores of times in Warrington, seen drunken men and women go into public houses and get served with more drink, and they are rarely ever refused as long as they have money to pay with. The plain fact is that the law is practically a dead letter in this respect in Warrington. Drunken- ne.ss abounds in the town, and brewers wax fat on the "unholy gains of this horrid traffic ;" they become" rich beyond the dreams of avarice" at the expense of all that is manliest and noblest in the poor people who are their victims. How many poor unfortunate fellows have been sent to prison for acts of violence committed under the influence of drink ! Had they been sober they would never have dreamed of committing such acts. And is nothing to be said for the poor children whoaretheprincipal sufferers by this evil ? Sir, if to protect the poor, and helpless, and suffering— those who have the greatest claim on our protection and sympa,hy—if this be coercion, then—like Oliver Twist —I for one shall ask for more.

~ PRO BONO PUBLICO. P.S.—I have seen a procession of poor miserable little creatures—made so, largely, by the drunken habits of their parents—the said drunken habits fostered and encouraged by" the trade,"—led by the Salvation Army through the streets on Walking Day, and I have wondered how any man of a tender and humane hear' could see such a sad sight and not feel that "the trade" was a terrible evil. Coercion. forsooth ! "WHO PAYS RATES ? "

Sir,—Last week an article appeared in the "Examiner" under the above heading written by "Economist." The article purports to be a reply to and contradiction of a statement made by me in an election speech at St. Peter's schoolroom last month. lam afraid the writer is not an all-round _economist. He seems to have been In a very loquacious mood, for his article is most verbose. It would have been much easier, less trouble, and far less enshrouded in mystery, had he condensed the column of small print into one-fourth of ordinary type,but perhaps he had so much space to fill, or he knew that by giving a plain ungarbled statement the points of delusion would have been detected by the working-clasFes. . . _ _

After all, in the interests of the- ratepayers, I feel obliged to " F?:"110Ttlist " for taking up the subject, whatever his object may have been, because the rate question and others pertaining to the government of this borough have risen to such an altitude of Injustice, that I think ventilation, discussion, and exposure are neces- sary. At the same time I am afraid that the answers of " Economist " are too "scientific" to touch the matter at the core, or to enlighten the people concerned. I proved clearly, and I believe satisfactorily to the audience, that all the new property erected within the last 12 or 14 years, together with the heavily-increased assessments upon all, both old and new, had so enlarged the rate collectable value of the borough, that a diffe- rence ought to be seen and felt by the ratepayers, and by the ratepayers I mean, all rent-payers, including the working-classes. "Economist" says that rates are neither higher nor lower than they were about 14 years ago. If he means the average amount charged per pound, that is true, for ever since 1857 the average rating has been about the same, ss. 10d. per £, but what about the increased assessment? I will cite the case I named in the school- room, and which " Economist " has made the subject of his article. The case I refer to is that a friend of mine whose shop, about 14 years ago, was assessed at £2O, but, is now raised to £6O; in other words, 14 years ago, his rates amounted to £5 16s. Bd., whereas, through the raising of his assessment, he is now paying £l7 10s., thus showing that ho actually pays an increase for the same shoo ef £ll 13s. 4d. If, therefore, one man, for one shop, pays this increase in 14 years, what must be the extra amount received by the borough from all the property in the town, including the rates collected from all the new property which I estimated as one-third, or about 33 per cent. increase? Again, what was the assessed value of the rates 14 years ago, and what are they now? Taking the Borough Treasurer's report. in 1874 the assessable value was £92,785, but in 1888 it has risen to £136,420. showing an undeniable increase of £43,635; that is 43,635 times ss. 10d., taking the last ten years' average. This shows a clear gain to the Borough every year, of £12,726 175.6 d. Surely even "Economist" will acknowledge that something ought to be shown from such a handsome yearly increased income, and that the ratepayers should feel it, more or less, in their ra'es and rents. Taking almost a month to criticise my statement, I should naturally have expected a far clearer, and better reply, especially since his answers are "scientifically deduced from a consideration of economic principles or laws." What does he say? Ist "That in the end all rates are a deduction from ground rents—from the value of the land upon which houses and other buildings are erected, and that working people, and indeed all people who live in houses, for which they pay rent, are never affected temporarily or permanently, by the increase or decrease of rates." Ind "He asserts that rates rarely have the effect of preventing property owners from securing fair profit, upos the money they invest in pro- perty.' 3rd, he can "easily prove that, in very many cases, rates are really paid out of the additional value Which has been conferred on building sites, not by the owners, but by the inhabitants." 'Economist" then asks the question "If rates were lowered and streets made at less cost, would the man who builds houses get the benefit of these reductions? It is very easy to ,see that he would not, for the only difference would be that the builder would then be able to pay a higher price for building sites." So much for " Economist's " scientific answers. The article extending to a column is thus reduced to a few lines. Let us just take his points seriatim. Ist "That all rates are a deduction from ground rents, and that neither owners nor occupiers are affected by the increase or decrease of rates." Take the shop I have instanced above, for an answer. The shop is an old one, and the ground rent was unalterably fixed when the land was leased, so that however the site may have been improved by central position, &c.,no matter who, or what may have been the cause, the shop has trebled in assessment. and the borough has the advantage of the rise ; but the increased rate cannot effect the landowner in any way during the 999 years for which it is leased. Upon whom then does the rate fall? Who would the bcrough sue, if the rates were net paid? It must be very clear to " Economist " from his own knowledge, that the rule is to sue the tenant. But' suppose for a moment, that the said shop had never been increased in its assessment from £5 16s. Bd. to £l7 10s., it must be as clear to " Economist " that. either the landlord or

tenant, or both, must be better in pocket to the tune of the increase £ll 13s. 44. per year. This, if fairly divided betweeh them, would increase the interest of the owner, and help the tenant so far if inclined to reduce the price of his goods, to compete with market business. I need not pursue this further, for the rule is the same al round. Before leaving this point however let me ask " Economist " where the rate comes from for Borough purposes? Do they corns from property or land ? If he does not own property, let him buy some, and he will soon be able to answer this question, and know that land is subject to Government taxes only.

2nd "That rates do not affect property owners interest." This on the surface appears to be correct, but why? Simply because the ten years' average rate per cent, have been kept about the same, only differing a halfpenny for the last 30 years. Let us look below the surface of " Economist's " arguments. Suppose for a moment that all the rates were cleared away, would not the landlord then be able to let his property at a corres- ponding per centage less? It is plain that he could, and still suffer no loss. On the other hand, suppose the rates were doubled per pound, he must then either suffer the loss by reduced per centage as interest, or he must raise the rents of his houses, thus throwing the loss upon his tenants, while the landowner in either case would remain at a legally fixed income.

3rd " Economist' can "easily prove that rates are paid out of the additional value of building sites." Let me I ask again where do Borough rates come from? And even independent of that hs must see that if a builder 1 puts up property at extra cost of land &c., he has con- sidered the outgo and what rent will be produced so as to secure a fair interest. Then in that case the extra site price must fall upon the tenant. The occupiers of cottages cannot fail to perceive, even if it does not strike "Economist" that a raising or lowering of the rates must inevitably affect their rents. If a cottage be erected with a view of producing a reasonable interest, and there be a considerable increase in the rates it cannot but be expected that the rent will rise in proportion, whereas in view of the competition of property owners, a reduction of rates must of necessity cause a corresponding reduction of rents. I give here facts and figures in contradistinction to the scientific arguments of "Economist." Had he employed a few statistics, the holl )wness of his arguments would have been only too apparent. I am sorry to have taken so much of your valuable space, but -I have condensed as much as possible. The question of rates, &c.. in Warrington I hope will be freely taken up both by the press, and by the rate- payers generally, strengthening their own hands by Joining the Association so actively at work in this good cause.—Yours H. THORNTON.

The Laurels, Fearnhead Cross, Nov. 21, 1888. [We are willing to allow discussion in the " Examiner " of this Important subject, but we must ask corres- pondents not to let each letter exceedione-third of a column in length.—En. Ex.J

Sir,—Your contributor "Economist," in his article last week, informs your readers that only persons who own land pay rates. The common opinion that rentpayers and property owners did go is altogether wrong. " Economist " says so, and being a wise writer must be right. It isquite true I have a number of receipts for rates on my file, but what do these prove? Why, that I have been robbed. Had there not better be called a public meeting of all people who have wrongly paid rates to demand a retnrn of their money at once? I would further suggest that "Economist" be one of the speakers. Please, Mr. Editor, give his name to the world so that he may be invited, and receive the honour so richly merited. When next the rate collector calls upon me I shall refer him to my landlord, and I recommend this course to your readers.—Yours truly, A GRATEFUL RATEPAYER.

Tr! P, EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 24, 1888.

DOMESTIC ECONOMY: OR, WIVES AND HUSBANDS. (From "Lays and Lyrics," by GEO. LANCASTER, Hull) PART 1. In those nice suburbs, cleanly built, and wide, Where drapers lodge, and bankers' clerks reside; Where the perambulating nursemaid drags Her chubby baby up and down the flags; Where rows of drawing-rooms politely blind The rows of kitchens out of sight behind; Whose windows show bright flowers that will not 1a Of never withering wire and cotton made; Where stucco towers of styles conglomerated, With porticos and pilasters are mated; Where genteel tradesmen, not quire tired of town. In easy circumstances, settle down To sniff the breezes wafted rich and sweet, From those trim gardens all along the street, ' Dwelt Robert Goodman, young, but staid and sage, Because he married at an early age. The lovely Lila WAS his blooming wife. And her he loved, aye, loved her as his life; Yet did be oft remark with serious air, . . Her heart was fickle, tho' her face was fair; For showy figures, fine and bearded faces, Were the best passports to her smiling graces; And what besides increased his painful state— Her dress was wasteful—her expenses great; And much he feared, as lengthening bills extend, That want and poverty would be his end. He might, with reason, feel some shades of fear. When six new bonnets scarce would last a year; He might, with reason, feel some slight dismay, When Jews and barbers ate up half his pay. Why, Wisdom? why? thou most contrary beldam, Dost thou in lovely heads reside so seldom? Yet she was learned, if she was not wise; „. For oh! 'twas grand to hear her moralise. Nice shades of vice and virtue she'd define, -• And mark the limits of the moral line ya With such precision, and with such good sense, Expressed and heightened with such eloquence, That Robin's anger melted into tears. He blanked his doubtings, and forgot his fears, Admired her beauty, owned her gentle sway, And the prepared reproof died unexpressed away. But Heaven, who preachers say inflicts the grief, Provides a balm to give the wound relief. Some comfort still is left to thwart despair, I If Lila's uncle leaves an ample share • Of the gold hoardings he has scraped together, By selling tripe, and buying bones and leather; Then may these awful reckonings be defrayed, And each rapacious creditor be paid. The miller then shall nod, the butcher The grocer bow in his accustcmed style; Experience then shall gift my wife with sense, To balance her incomings, and expense; p;of To pay in cash, to keep a fund in store, And gad about with senseless men no more. A thought like this his ardent soul exalts, Nor could he rage to see such hopeful faults. He calms his fears, and bids his doubtings cease, And makes a fresh resolve to keep the peace. Complaints, he knew, would only prove a cur se, - To stir up strife, and make the matter worse. But ah! how oft determinations fail! And good resolves are made, of no avail! When kings and queens are secretly ajar, A slight dispute will soon become a war; When gunpowder is hid beneath the rock, A little spark will give th' explosive shock; So little things,(when discontent is rife, Will soon create a breach 'twixt man and wife. This, even Robin will consent to own, When one cross word could bring such mischief down. It chanced one morning as they sat at meat. The bread was burnt and very tough to eat. Long time poor Robin tugged, and gnawed, and chewed, Till tired at last, ark angry oath ensued. "The deuce," cried he, "I well may gnaw and pull, 'Twill take some time to get one's belly full Of this vile food; for once, I've had enough; Let rats and pigs devour the cursed stuff; • To dogs and roosters let the mess be flung, On heaps of ashes, or on hills of dung." • "Nay, swear not so," said Lila, touched with shame, "The bread is bad, but I am not to blame. 'Twas my friend Rachel came across the way, To show me her new head-dress, yesterday, Who, with such lively gossip, filled my head, AS made me totally forget my bread, But Robin, if you were a man of thought, You'd hire a cook to help me as you ought. How can I answer every duteous call. And only one young lass to help in all? just a slave—but why that angry look ? t I tell you, Robin, we must have a cook." "A cook !" cried Robin, "what to do. I pray? And who's to feed her? who's to find the pay ?" He spoke severely, but 'twas all he said; He bit his lip, and sadly shook his head, . And inly wished he never had been wed.

" Ah ! monstrous man," the wrathful wife replied, " Ah ! monstrous man," and as she spoke she cried, "Since such request (alas that I should cry), So simply asked, should meet with such reply. When Morning-callers come. I think it hard My taper fingers should be daubed with lard. At music too, I just begin to play, And spoiling puddings hasten me away. When friends drink tea, the shame I keenly feel— 'Tis I must bake, and I prepare the meal: The self-same cause conspires my rest to cheat, For I must rise that you may breakfast eat. Can well-bred folks submit to things like these? Or churlish men deny to women ease?" Then Robin rose in haste, and banged his chair, .• And out he rushed, to breathe the outer air. For who can sit and hear with calm content, When angry ladies give their feelings vent? At once he thought he would his troubles end In a deep stream; but first he sought his friend— His constant friend, who loved a dry old game At chess or cards; Dick Horner was his name. Now Dick was smoking in his easy chair, • y.f., And sipping sherry of a vintage rare, As was his wont, to wile the time away, . When none of his companions came to play. For wine (as topers tell us l has the power To yield delight for many a lonely hour; Wine bids the transient fires of rapture rise, And calls forth joyous sparks from tearful eyes; Wine gives the strength (so epicureans say) - -To eat three monstrous dinners in a day; And wine, a mighty beverage, is able To stretch big men beneath the dinner table. No wonder then, when Robin 'gan to sup, He soon gave all his thoughts of drowning up. The first deep draught he took subdued his grief, The second brought a little more relief; If any cares were left his peace to pester. They soon gave way, for Dick was a great jester. He spent much time, like many wittier folks, In bottling genius from a book of jokes; And here, Dick's temper needs a few comments, That we may understand the next events. Sagacious, solemn, penetrating, sly, And full of speeches which were curt and dry; His manner, with a stranger would offend. But still a merry fellow with his friend. Two nice estates, of moles and mortgage clear, That brought a thousand golden pounds a year, For all his multifarious wants provide; (Left by an uncle o his mother's side). This would have made him, had his heart been tender, A mighty favourite with the gentler gender; But, too much study, lam grieved to say, •.. Had turned his notions a peculiar way. He had a deep and calculating mind,. With philosophic theories refined. His soul had soared on speculative wings, To view th' eternal fitnesses of things, * And when each premise had been gravely cast, He formed this strange conclusion at the last— That women were the sole and cursed source Of moral evil in the universe. Oft would he say, when pressed to take a wife— " Keep clear of ladies if you value life; Be not deceived with all their airs and graces, Their artful manners, and their pretty faces; These are but lures to draw the unwary wight, Who looks with wistful eyes upon the sight, And thinks (mistaken man) a pretty wife Would make him happy for the rest of life. But when one year has more experience brought. His home, he finds, is not the heaven he thought. Scolds, quarrels, debts, and many a noisome thing, Soon make him rue the day he bought the ring. So, when some hungry hornet sniffs from far, The savoury vapours of a treacle jar, He longs to taste—and tasting, quickly feels The miry mixture sticking to his heels. In vain for me the treacherous nets are spread— I know the dodge; I'm far too wise too wed." Then, thus to Robin, in a bantering way— "l notice thu art very grave to-day, In spite of wino; say now what ails thee lad? • I thought you married folk were never sad. Come now, be candid, and the truth disclose, Perhaps thy cares I may remove—who knows? Some matrimonial strife has happed, I ween. Perchance hast broken Lilm's crinoline, And heard the subject well enlarged upon? - Or crushed her hat? Or spoilt her new chignon ?" Bob soon replied—"! know your cast of mind, I know your enmity to woman kind. Once I believed (in visionary youth) That women were all purity, and truth. And kind endurance, gentleness, and duty; -*- I always joined good sense to female beauty; But the sad trials that I now endure, Have altered my opinions, to be sure." Dick laughed aloud, and clapped his hands with 0, " What ! have I made a convert, too, of thee?" "Nay, far," said Robin, "far from me indeed, , To keep the points of your detested creed. .

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CAN-AL.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CAN-AL.

MOORE TO STOCKTON HEATH. The recent stormy weather has considerably retarded the outdoor work during the week, and although the gales have done only a trifling amount of damage, the men have several times had to cease work for short Deriod.s on account of the violence of the storm. On fuesday the force of the gale was almost sufficknt to blow anyone walking along the path on the bank, into the cutting. At Moore only one steam navvy is at work, and no more are met with until up to the end of the cutting at Acton Grange is reached. At Moore espe- cially, and in other portions of the cutting, the rain has lodged in such quantities that an increase in the work done by the pumps will be necessary to remove it. Two steam navvies are at work at Town Field, where they will soon reach the Chester-road, the preliminary steps to closing which, are, we believe, being taken. The German navvy at Stockton Heath is removing a sur- prising amount of soil in a very short time, and is visited by large.numbenf people.

div.head: 'ENTERTAINMENt AT ACTON GRANGE. __ _
div.p: 'ENTERTAINMENt AT ACTON GRANGE. __ _

On Monday evening, a service of song entitled " Eva,' was given in the Mission Hall, Acton Grange, by mem- bers of the Working Men's Mission, Bank Quay. There was a very large attendance of navvies, with their wives and children, by whom the entertainment, which was very well rendered, seemed heartily appreciated. At the conclusion, the performers were heartily thanked by the audience, on the proposition of Mr. Waddington, the missionary. DARESBURY HIGHWAY BOARD AND THE CANAL. Yesterday afternoon at a meeting of the Daresbury Highway Board, presided over by Mr. E. Greenall, Mr. J. R. Walker, on behalf of Mr. T. A. Walker, contractor of the Ship Canal, applied for permission to divert the traffic on the Chester road along the new road which runs from near Lower Walton into the Northwich-road at Stockton Heath. It was explained by the Clerk that this application was necessary because it was laid down in the Board's clauses in the Ship Canal Act that before the Chester-road was diverted the Ship Canal Com- pany must complete a new road from Lower Walton , to Stockton Heath, and also another new road from Lower Walton across Arpley Meadows to Wilderspool causeway. This latter road It was stated had not yet been begun with. Mr. J. R. Walker and Mr. 0. Brooks, (who represented the Canal engineer) were in attend- nee on the Board.—Mr. Parr remarked that there was a rumour that the Ship Canal Company did not intend to make the road across Arpley meadows at all if they could get out of it. (Laughter.)—ln answer to a ques- tion Mr. Walker said he could not tell when the road across Arpley meadows would be completed.—Mr. Parr spoke against granting the application till the Canal Company had complied with the Act of Parliament.— Mr. J. Darbyshire spoke to the same effect and said that there was already more than sufficient traffic on the Northwich-road through Stockton Heath and Wilders- pool. He moved that the application be not granted.— Mr. T. S. Burgess seconded this proposal which was agreed to.—An application for permission to lay a line of rails across Grappenhall-road to the south of Latch- ford station was granted subject to certain conditions for the safety of passengers.
WYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL MISSION.

An eight days' mission in connection with Wycliffe Congregational Church, Bewsey-st., was commenced on Sunday morning, and has been con- tinua during the week. It will be brought to a conclusion to-morrow (Sunday). The Rev. John Yonge, pastor, is the missioner, and when he preached at the opening service of the mission his discourse was attentively listened to by a large con- gregation. Ile took his text from the words.— "Come from the four winds, 0 breath," Ezekiel xxxvii.. part of the 9th verse. In the course of his remarks the preacher said that all spiritual workers had to learn that no condition in which men could be found was hopeless to God: that he took as a lesson standing out inthe very forefront of the vision or parable under consideration that morning. In the mission which was about to be held in connection with that church they were going to try to make the spiritually dead hear the voice of the Son of God, to try to bring Christian professors out of the graves of self-indulgence, worldly desires, and moral indifference, and to try to bring sinners and unbelievers around them, to hear that they might live. He did not believe that the age of preaching was past; the pulpit still possessed a power from on high. The message of the Gospel had not lost its interest for men, and if only it be faithfully get before them by a living church and an honest ministry, the truth of Christ could yet secure an audience, even from the unlikeliest sources. The con- gregation must make it their endeavour to carry home the message of the mission—that not only the deaf, but the very dead should hear. Though preaching had its own remarkable power,there was a limit beyond which it could not go. No voice but God's could really make itself heard in the valley of death. Only Christ could make the dead Lazarus come back. l'aul might plant, and Apollos water, but it was only God who could give the increase. Man might do his best, but it would be as nothing until inspired by the Almighty spirit. Here, then, was there need for prayer. Here, too, in all likelihood, they might finel a reason why their preaching and teaching in the past had resulted in so little. He re-iterated that morn- ing the request for prayer from every member of the church and congregation. No doubt some of them might look upon the request as a piece of moral religious con- vention:- lism—a request that was seemly to make under the circumstances, but one which had in it no real, sincere earnestness, for them. Let that idea be dismissed, as a steadfast, believing offering of their prayer was truly, as his was, indispensable to the success of the mission. At the evening service, which was also well attended, Mr. W. H. Wallington sang the solo "I am praying for you." During the week a special service has been held each evening, the pulpit being occupied by the Rev. John Yonge. The Nev. J. Davies, of Cock- hedge, and the Rev. J. Bedell, of Lymm, have also taken part in the services. The subject of the discourse on Monday evening was "The Wages of Sin," and Miss Mary Podmore sang the solo "Nothing but Leaves." On Tuesday evening "The Cross of Christ" was the subject, and Mrs. A. H. Lee sang "He was Despised." Mr. Yonge spoke on the words "Repent and Believe the Gospel," on Wednesday evening, and Miss Roberts sang "Seeking to Save" as a solo. On Thursday evening Mr. W. Brown sang "Why not To-night," and the subject of the missioner was " Life or Death, Which? Choose Life." Last evening Mr. Yonge discoursed on "The Perils of Delay," and Miss Paul sang a solo. Miss Edith Walling- ton will sing the solo at the service to be held this (Saturday) evening, and it is expected that Mrs. Pearson will sine at the service on Sunday evening. Between three and four hundred people have attended each I service. need ems

An entertain- ment was provided by Miss Radcliffe, Mrs Carter, Mr. Hope and Mr. Edwards. Mrs. Eccles presided at the pianoforte.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

TRANSFER OF LICENSE.-At the Altrincham Petty Sessions, on Monday, an application for the transfer of the license of the Railway Hotel, Heatley, from Nellie M. Steel to John James Harrop, was granted. WESLEYAN CHAPEL Caorre. A social evening was spent on Wednesday in the schoolroom by the mem- bers of the Wesleyan Chapel Choir and friends. he proceedings of the evening took the form of a con- versazione, and were highly successful. During the evening a programme of pianoforte solos. songs, read- ings, and recitations was gone through, interspersed with games which were kept up until a late hour.

LiiM MIJTITAL IMIPROVEaMEN'T SOCIETY.—The Weekly meeting of this society was held in the Drill Hall, Lymm, on Monday evening', there being a good attendance. Mr. John Knowles presided, and the secretary, Mr. John Brearley, introduced a discussion on "Intemperance: How shall we grapple wi:h it ?" A warm discussion followed, in which Messrs. R. Dutton, J. Dodds, J. Mort, Gillanders, F. 0. Moston, and the Chairman took part. ITEM DISTRICT ANIk THE COUNTY COUNCIL.—It is announced Mr. Charles Lister, of Agden Hall, Lymm. has consented to become the candidate for the Lymm district of the county of Chester, which comprises the parishes of Lymm, High Leigh, Bollington' Agden, Miilington, Rostheme, Ashley, Warburton, and Carring- , ton. At present there is no other candidate in the field, and in the event of a contest Mr. Lister would receive the support of the local Conservative Association.

div.head: LIBERAL MEETING AT LYMM.
div.p: LIBERAL MEETING AT LYMM.

- A well-attended meeting was held at the Plough Hotel, on Wednesday evening, in support of the candidature for the Altrincham Division, in the Liberal interest, of Mr. I. S. Leadam. Mr. J. A. Swanwick, in the absence of Mr. John Rylands, occupied the chair, amongst those also present were Lord Monkswell, Mr. I S. Leaclam, Mr. T. Stelfox, and others.—After the Chairman had spoken, Mr. G. L. Welford proposed, and Mr. Robert Lewis seconded a resolution to the effect that the present mutual relations of Great Britain on the one hand and Ireland on the other tend to disruption of the empire; that an entire change in these relations was imperatively demanded, and the establishment of a subordinate Parliament in Dublin for the encouragement of all Irish local affairs was absolutely essential before the numerous reforms so much needed on this side of the channel can be taken in hands.—Lord Monkswell, who supported the resolution, said that he was by no means crushed at the prospect they had before them of entering into a crusade against the highly-placed classes of this country, for he said, they had almost invariably found that the great,

rich, and highly-placed people had been proved to be totally and entirely in the wrong, and that the masses of the people had been proved to be totally and entirely in the right. The Tories at the present time were undoubtedly in an unfortunate position. The real old Tory knew very well that he was on the high way to become extinct. The Tories were a doomed race; they were being hunted down; they had the natural instincts of the hunted animal, and were the artful dodgers of politics. (Laughter and cheers.) The present Government represented themselves, as it were, to be Pharisees—they were a perfectly righteous people —but if they looked properly into the matter they might find themselves to be in the position of the repen- tant publican. (Laughter.) The dissentient Liberals knew that the Home Rule party was winning all along , the line, and it was absurd to find how they picked up crumbs of comfort anywhere. They must, indeed, be hard up. (Laughter.) The great speech of Mr. Glad- stone at Birmingham had crushed the last hope of the dissentient Liberal and the Tory party. (Cheers.) The significance of that speech was that it showed the un- diminished vitality of their great leader. (Cheers.) The position of their opponents was like that of the old lady who appealed to the captain of a vessel in a storm, and was told hat she must "Trust in Providence." Said the old lady, "Isit so bad as that ?" (Laughter.) The Irish people, Lord Monkswell continued, were singularly amenable to kind treatment, and the Liberal party intended to go on treating them kindly. (Cheers.)—Mr. Leadam also supported the resolution, and referred at considerable length to speeches recently delivered by Sir W. C. Brookes, and to the Irish question.—The proposi- tion was unanimously agreed to. and a vote of thanks to the chairman for presiding brought the meeting to a close.

div.p: LATEST NEWS.
WARRINGTON AND THE COUNTY COUNCIL.

The following communication has been made to the Mayor with regard to the representation of Warrington in the new County Council : Dear Mr. Mayor,—lt has been represented to us by persons taking an active part in political affairs on both sides that it is desirable there should be no contest in the election of members for the County Council, and we agree in this opinion. The following names have been suggested to us as Being generally acceptable, and having ourselves made inquiries we find this to be the case : FRANK A. ROBERTS, JOHN WHITE, FREDERICK MONKS.

We have therefore concluded to communicate with you, and to say that we are prepared to support these gentlemen. H. BLECKLY. PETER STUBS. JOHN RYLANDS. JOHN G. McMINNIES. The Worshipful, The Mayor, Warrington, November 23rd.

THE IRISH MURDERER "SKIN THE GOAT" EARLESTOWN.—The Irish " Invincible " known as "Skin the Goat," whose connection with the Phcenix Park murders will be well remembered. was one of a gang of four prisoners who passed through Earlestown on Tuesday forenoon. They were being conveyed in a special carriage from Fleetwood to London, it is stated, for the purpose of giving evidence in connection with the Parnell Commission. They were in charge of a number of prison warders, but they could not be observed, as the blinds of the windows were all down. The carriage was attached to the train arriving from Wigan at 10.40, and ,at Earlestown the carriage was transferred to the train leaving at 10.45 for War- rington and the South. , EARLESTOWN CONSERVATIVE CLUB.—A pleasant gathering was held in the Conservative Club, Earlestown. on Friday night, on the occasion of a "smoking concert," and presentation of prizes, won by members in a recent billiard handicap. The first , prize, a handsome silver-mounted billiard cue and case, presented by Mr. T. H. Pearson. was handed I to Mr. James Foden ; the second prize, a cue and case, presented by Messrs. Orme and Sons, was secured by Mr. C. Guinness; and four smaller prizes were won by Messrs. J. Stacey, H. Boardman, H. J. Longton, and W. Aspinall. During the even- ing an excellent programme of songs, &c., was gone through. Selections of music were contri- buted by Messrs, R. Wright, G. Bailey, W. Walton, F. Brierley, &c., a recitation by Mr. W. Sutton; a violin solo by Mr. T. Lewis, and a dulcimer solo by Mr. R. Sutton.

Mitchell, of Golborne, the :use of the local Liberals. Mr. J. Unsworthe jun., presided and there was a fair attendance. Mr. Mitchell had generously placed the building a'S their disposal for the nominal rent of £lO Per annum. Several speakers followed, after which thil shares (.E1 each) were offered to the audience, an at the close the Secretary announced that up to they' period 122 shares had been allotted. A resolution. thanking Mr. Mitchell for his continued support t! the Liberal party, and pledging the meeting to giv• the undertaking all the financial aid possible, Wag enthusiastically adopted.

CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL. TO THE ELECTORS OF THE APPLETON DIVISION. LAVIES AND GENTLEMEN,—A wish having been expressed the I should offer myself as a Candidate for the Appleton Division of the County Council, I beg to offer my services. and at the same time to assure the Ratepayers that, if they should honour me with their suffrages, it would be my earnest desire to promote the Interests of the County, and especially of the Appleton Division, by every means in soy power, and to give careful attention to the duties of the position which I may be elected to fill. Having been for some years a member of the Finance Committee, and other- wise conversant with County business, I trust I may be con- sidered competent to represent and to watch over your interests in this very important and responsible Council. I have the honour to be. Yours faithfully, • J. CHARLTON PARR. Grappenhall Reyes, Warrington, Nov. 22nd, 1888.

COUNTY COUNCIL FOR CHRBHIRR. To THE ELECTORS OF THE NORTH DIVISION OF RUNCORN. LADIES and GENTLEmas.—It is my intention to offer myself as a candidate, in the forthcoming election of a member to represent your division on the new County Council. On a future date I Will address you more fully as to my opinions, and also as to the objects I should have in view in seeking to be returned as a member of the Council. I am, Ladies and gentlemen. Yours faithfully, W. H. LINAICHR. '5B, Righ-street, Runcorn, 21st Nov., 1888.

My faith was foolish, yours is twice as bad, And men, you know, in changing faiths, are mad; They wake, they rise from one delusive dream, And rush into the opposite extreme. As when the driver, with unpractised hands, Avoids the corner where the lamp-post stands, He pulls away, but ftulls so monstrous wide, He hits the ditch upon the other side. Not b 0 with me; the former faith has gone. Yet never will I take your gloomy one, But find some middle point of hope instead. This morn we quarrelled—all about the bread; Yet why should I recite in vulgar phrase, The sad detail of Lila's careless ways? She's vexed me sorely; and I pray you Dick, To lend me your assistance in a trick. When night's dark curtain shroud's the heavenly d On wooden stretcher you shall bear me home, All wet, and soaked, and motionless, and dead, As newly grappled from the river's bed. Then will I learn, by all the ways I can, In part from you, as you're a truthful man, In part myself from what I see and hear, If any love is left, if any grief sincere, To make me hope that folly will give way, And common sense resume her cheerful sway." Before he finished, Richard's head was bent With ready nods, in token of consent. The morning passed with fresh relays of wine, Together then they lunch, together dine. Oft Richard joked, and often strove to vex His married friend, by railing at the sex. "Oh, find me one, he cried, "unspoiled by pride, Who holds no code of fashion for her guide; Who does not paint, who marries not for pelf, Who keeps a piece of scandal to herself; Her will 1 wed; and wedding, will agree To love her just as much as she loves me; For marriage is a bird-cage.fußof blue-birds. Who bring around the cage alot of new birds, To get inside, the new birds beat about, But all the blue-birds struggle to get out." (To be continued.)

FRODSHAM. ACCIDENT.—On Tuesday an accident happened to a man named George Bailey, who, with others, was sheltering himself on the Frodsham Marsh from a heavy. shower behind a pile of sleepers. One of the sleepers was dislodged by the wind, and it fell heavily on Bailey's foot, fracturing his ankle severely. LECTURE AT KINGSLEY.—On Tuesday evening a lecture was delivered in the boy's school-room by the Rev. R. H. Maddox, on behalf of the Church of England Zenana Missionary Society. The Vicar (the Rev. A. P. Reynolds) presided. The interest in the lecture was further enhanced by means of a powerful oxy-hydrogen lantern, illustrating different subjects in connection with India and her people.

Lord Derby declines to become a candidate, as re- quested, for the Prescot division of the County Council. Mr. Christopher Sykes, M.P. will not resign his seat for the present, but it is understood he will not seek te- election at the end of the present parliament A Dundee telegram states that Ward Foundary, belong- ing to Messrs. Carmichael, was partially destroyed by fire on Friday morning. The damage is estimated at £15,000. William Jamieson for many years tho champion wrestler in the Cumberland and Westmoreland style died yesterday at the Griffin Inn, Penrith, in his fifty- eighth year. On Friday morning it was stated that Mr. Bright passed a rather bad night, with no improvement in his condition. A telegram received last evening states that Mr. Bright's condition is unchanged. PROSECUTION OF NATIONALIST M.P.',—The " Dublin Express" states the Attorney-General has issued orders for the prosecution of seven members of Parliament— Messrs. Finucane, John O'Connor, Sheehy, Mayne, Condor, P. O'Brien, and Dr. Tanner—for intimidating individuals who took derelict farms. THE IRISH LAND BILL.—The minority which opposed' the second reading of the Irish Land Purchase Bill was composed of 157Gladstonian Liberals, including Mr. John Morley and Sir William Harcourt, and 69 Nationalists. The majority was composed of 255 Conservatives and 46 Liberal Unionists. THE PARNELL INQUlRY.—District Inspector Huggins, of Castle Island, occupied the witness box at the Parnell Commission during the greater part of yesterday. He detailed the number of outrages which took place in the district between 1886 and 1888, but admitted, in cross- examination, that sham outrage,s were sometimes got up by tenants themselves to avoid payment of rent, or for some other purposes. ANOTHER TERRIBLE MURDER IN IRELAND.—Denis Daley, a well-to-do farmer, was found murdered on Thursday night, on the road at Glounageenthy, half- way between Tralee and Castleisland. He had six bullet wounds—four in the breast and two in the head, and appeared to have been returning from a turf bog, when he was waylaid and shot down. Two persons have been arrested, one being a brother and the other a relative of the deceased's wife. Several other arrests are expected. ALARMING MINING ACCIDENT. One hundred miners engaged at llalkyn Lead mine near Holywell were imprisoned in the mine for several hours yesterday owing to a break down of the winding engine. Eventually they made the:7 escape by wading two miles through a draining tunnel against a strong current of water which was up to their shoulders. YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—FRIDAY. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. QUESTIONS, &C.—The POSTMASTER-GENERAL, in an- swer to Mr. Fenwick. said the rule prohibiting officeri of the post-office from taking any active part in con- tested Parliamentary eleetions must be held to apply to the election of County Councillors.—The Home SECRE- TARY, replying to Mr. Hunter, said he was quite pre- pared to offer a pardon to any accomplice in other cases than that of Kelly, the woman murdered in Whitechapel.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, re- plying to Mr. Causton, said the Wheel Tax was not required. THE IRISH LAND BILL.—On motion to go into Com- mittee on-the Land Purchase Ireland Bill, Mr. PARNELL moved it be an instruction to the committee that they have power to provide that the Irish Land Commission may take an account of the amount of arrears of rent due ; tenants desirous of purchasing holdings who have made applications and judicial rents fixed for their holdings, s and may decide where whole or any or what part of such arrears ought to be paid. He urged the House to accept the instruction. Mr. WADDY seconded the amendment, and Mr. W. SMITH opposed the. instruction. The Government had reason to believe that the Commissioners would not permit any transaction whiCh was harsh to the tenant. M. Dimon supported and Mr. Pr..mixErr opposed the amen(' - ment. Mr. GLADSTONE said Mr. Smith had entirely passed over the main and principal contention that had been urged in favour of amendment. The arrears con- stituted a lever in the hands of the landlord to compel the tenant to give an unfair price. The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER justified the rejection of instiuction. After further discussion, Mr. Parnell's instruction was rejected by 182 to 148. [LEFT SITTING].
